Training Latent Diffusion Models with Interacting Particle Algorithms

The paper’s statements first; additional assumptions and new theorems second. Mathematics and exact Lean code appear side by side.

Published source; corrected checked proofs and new theory

The correspondence uses arXiv:2505.12412v3, the camera-ready version of the AISTATS 2026 paper, identical to the manuscript audited here. All 19 source results are proved in corrected form under the paper's assumptions A1–A4 and the added regularity R1–R7. The corrections and the new theory (explicit error budget, minibatch scaling, model bias and accuracy choices) are unpublished. The source audit records the corrected minibatch scaling and a counterexample to universal time-zero density regularity.

  • Tim Y. J. Wang, Juan Kuntz, and O. Deniz Akyildiz (2026). Training Latent Diffusion Models with Interacting Particle Algorithms. Proceedings of The 29th International Conference on Artificial Intelligence and Statistics, Proceedings of Machine Learning Research 300, 2791–2799. Audited version: arXiv:2505.12412v3

Part I — Results from the paper

Paper assumptions — A1–A4

Write a=(θ,ϕ)a=(\theta,\phi)a=(θ,ϕ), Um(a,z)=−log⁡p~a(xm,z)U_m(a,z)=-\log\tilde p_a(x^m,z)Um​(a,z)=−logp~​a​(xm,z), Zm(a)=∫e−Um(a,z) dzZ_m(a)=\int e^{-U_m(a,z)}\,dzZm​(a)=∫e−Um​(a,z)dz, and πam=Zm(a)−1e−Um(a,⋅)dz\pi_a^m=Z_m(a)^{-1}e^{-U_m(a,\cdot)}dzπam​=Zm​(a)−1e−Um​(a,⋅)dz. The evidence and energy are

ℓ(a)=1M∑mlog⁡Zm(a),F(a,q)=−ℓ(a)+1M∑mKL(qm∥πam).\ell(a)=\frac1M\sum_m\log Z_m(a),\qquad F(a,q)=-\ell(a)+\frac1M\sum_m\mathrm{KL}(q^m\|\pi_a^m).ℓ(a)=M1​m∑​logZm​(a),F(a,q)=−ℓ(a)+M1​m∑​KL(qm∥πam​).

Here ℓ\ellℓ and FFF abbreviate the paper's tilted evidence ℓ~\widetilde\ellℓ and energy F~\widetilde FF. The source cards below retain tildes. In the model-bias theorem in Part II, ℓ\ellℓ explicitly denotes the original, untilted evidence.

The paper uses the normalized product distance d((a,q),(b,r))2=∥a−b∥2+M−1∑mW2(qm,rm)2d((a,q),(b,r))^2=\|a-b\|^2+M^{-1}\sum_m W_2(q^m,r^m)^2d((a,q),(b,r))2=∥a−b∥2+M−1∑m​W2​(qm,rm)2, with M>0M>0M>0. The law qmq^mqm is the latent posterior approximation for datum mmm; NNN is the particle count per datum. The optimizer targets tilted evidence, not automatically the original likelihood.

A1 — Model regularity

assump:model_reg · main_aistats.tex:143–150

Mathematical statement

Put a=(θ,ϕ)a=(\theta,\phi)a=(θ,ϕ), ρ~a(z)=p~a(x,z)\tilde\rho_a(z)=\tilde p_a(x,z)ρ~​a​(z)=p~​a​(x,z), and π~a(z)=ρ~a(z)/Aa\tilde\pi_a(z)=\tilde\rho_a(z)/A_aπ~a​(z)=ρ~​a​(z)/Aa​. For every zzz, the maps a↦π~a(z)a\mapsto\tilde\pi_a(z)a↦π~a​(z) and a↦Aaa\mapsto A_aa↦Aa​ are differentiable. For every aaa, the spatial map z↦π~a(z)z\mapsto\tilde\pi_a(z)z↦π~a​(z) is C2C^2C2, and ρ~a(z)>0\tilde\rho_a(z)>0ρ~​a​(z)>0 everywhere.

Here AaA_aAa​ is the model's normalizing constant. The regularity contract records these conditions; it does not establish differentiation under integrals or boundary integration by parts.

import Mathlib.Analysis.Calculus.ContDiff.Defs
import Mathlib.Analysis.Calculus.Deriv.Basic
import Mathlib.MeasureTheory.Measure.ProbabilityMeasure
import Mathlib.MeasureTheory.Function.LpSeminorm.Defs
import Mathlib.Analysis.Convex.Strong
import Mathlib.Analysis.Calculus.Gradient.Basic

/-!
# Literal source regularity contracts

These are assumption translations, not existence theorems. In particular the
paper's universal solution premise includes strictly positive classical densities
at time zero even for arbitrary finite-second-moment initial laws. It is recorded
literally so that this strength is visible; it is not inferred from the other
source assumptions or used to hide an analytic bridge.
-/

noncomputable section

namespace LatentDiffusion.SourceAssumptions

open MeasureTheory Set
open scoped NNReal

variable {P Z : Type*} [NormedAddCommGroup P] [NormedSpace ℝ P]
  [NormedAddCommGroup Z] [NormedSpace ℝ Z]

/-- The source's normalized tilted posterior, with the normalizing constant
provided as model data. Normalization and existence of this constant are part of
the model interpretation, not proved by the regularity contract. -/

/-- The manuscript's model-regularity assumption. Parameter differentiability is
pointwise in the latent state; spatial regularity is pointwise in the parameter. -/

/-- The time-space domain in the source's C^{1,2} density assumption. -/

/-- Explicit partial derivatives and their joint continuity on the closed positive
time half-space. Time derivatives at zero are right derivatives, not derivatives
of an extension to negative time. This is the C^{1,2} meaning used here. -/

variable [MeasurableSpace Z]

/-- All data in a source classical solution. `flowEquation` is the actual gradient
flow equation chosen by the application, rather than a scalar energy estimate.
The density is required to realize the initial law as well as later laws. -/

/-- Literal universal solution-regularity premise: every parameter and every
finite-second-moment initial probability law admits the classical solution above.
This includes the source's density regularity and positivity at t=0. -/

section Potential

variable {H I : Type*} [NormedAddCommGroup H] [InnerProductSpace ℝ H] [CompleteSpace H]

/-- The source's joint strong-log-concavity premise, expressed for each negative
log tilted density `U i` in the full parameter-latent pair space. -/

/-- The source's differentiable joint log-likelihood and positive global
gradient-Lipschitz constant. Negating a log density preserves this bound. -/

end Potential

end LatentDiffusion.SourceAssumptions

Exact statement as printed in the paper
\begin{restatable}[Model regularity]{assumption_app}{modelregularityrestatable}\label{assump:model_reg}
    We assume that
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item For all $z \in \sZ$, $(\theta,\phi) \mapsto \tilde\pi_{\theta,\phi}(z)$ and $(\theta, \phi) \mapsto A_{\theta, \phi}$ are differentiable;
        \item for all $(\theta,\phi) \in \Theta \times \Phi$, $\tilde\pi_{\theta,\phi}$ is twice continuously differentiable;
        \item $\tilde{\rho}_{\theta,\phi}(z)>0$ for all $z\in \sZ$ and $(\theta,\phi) \in \Theta \times \Phi$.
    \end{enumerate}
\end{restatable}
Paper assumption / source result

A2 — Classical solutions for every initial law

assump:solution_reg · main_aistats.tex:151–154

Mathematical statement

For every parameter a0a_0a0​ and every collection μ01:M∈P2(Z)M\mu_0^{1:M}\in\mathcal P_2(Z)^Mμ01:M​∈P2​(Z)M, the source assumes a classical solution of its gradient flow with those initial values. The parameter path is C1C^1C1 on [0,∞)[0,\infty)[0,∞). Each law remains in P2(Z)\mathcal P_2(Z)P2​(Z) and has a positive Lebesgue density qtm(z)q_t^m(z)qtm​(z), jointly C1,2C^{1,2}C1,2 in time and space on [0,∞)×Z[0,\infty)\times Z[0,∞)×Z.

The Lean contract uses a supplied reference measure ν\nuν, instantiated by Lebesgue measure, and the actual flow equation as an explicit predicate. Its C1,2C^{1,2}C1,2 contract requires continuous first time derivatives and first and second spatial derivatives, including right time derivatives at zero.

Source issue. The universal quantifier includes singular initial laws, while the density and positivity conditions include t=0t=0t=0. This premise is displayed literally and is not claimed to follow from A1, A3 or A4. The source audit records the resulting limitation.

Exact statement as printed in the paper
\begin{restatable}[Regularity of solutions]{assumption_app}{solutionregularityrestatable}\label{assump:solution_reg}
    For any initial conditions $(\theta, \phi, q^{1:M})\in \mathcal{M}^{1:M}$,  the gradient flow has a classical solution $(\theta_t, \phi_t,  q_t^{1:M})_{t \geq 0}$ with $(\theta_0, \phi_0, q_0^{1:M}) = (\theta, \phi, q^{1:M})$.  
Furthermore, for all $m\in [M]$ and $t \geq 0$, $q_t^m$ has a Lebesgue density in $\mathcal{C}^{1,2}([0, \infty) \times \sZ, \mathbb{R}^+)$ and $(\theta_t, \phi_t) \in \mathcal{C}^1([0, \infty), \Theta \times \Phi)$.
\end{restatable}
Paper assumption / source result

A3 — Joint strong log-concavity

assump:strong_log_concave · main_aistats.tex:155–157

Mathematical statement

For every datum mmm, the tilted joint density is λ\lambdaλ-strongly log-concave in the full pair (a,z)(a,z)(a,z), with one λ>0\lambda>0λ>0. Equivalently, for Um(a,z)=−log⁡p~a(xm,z)U_m(a,z)=-\log\tilde p_a(x^m,z)Um​(a,z)=−logp~​a​(xm,z),

Um(sx+(1−s)y)≤sUm(x)+(1−s)Um(y)−λ2s(1−s)∥x−y∥2,0≤s≤1.U_m(sx+(1-s)y)\le sU_m(x)+(1-s)U_m(y)-\tfrac\lambda2s(1-s)\|x-y\|^2,\quad 0\le s\le1.Um​(sx+(1−s)y)≤sUm​(x)+(1−s)Um​(y)−2λ​s(1−s)∥x−y∥2,0≤s≤1.

The particle-average geometry used below is normalized in the latent coordinates. The same constant does not hold in an unweighted replicated Euclidean norm without accounting for that normalization.

A4 — Joint Lipschitz gradient

assump:lipschitz_grad · main_aistats.tex:200–207

Mathematical statement

Every UmU_mUm​ is differentiable and, for one L>0L>0L>0,

∥∇Um(a,z)−∇Um(a′,z′)∥≤L∥(a,z)−(a′,z′)∥.\|\nabla U_m(a,z)-\nabla U_m(a',z')\|\le L\|(a,z)-(a',z')\|.∥∇Um​(a,z)−∇Um​(a′,z′)∥≤L∥(a,z)−(a′,z′)∥.

Negating the log tilted density leaves the Lipschitz constant unchanged. The source's discretization theorem additionally assumes Lipschitz gradients of the tilting penalty R\mathcal RR; the numerical results below instead expose the complete force and its approximation error directly.

paper's universal solution premise includes strictly positive classical densities

104structure LipschitzGradient (U : I → H → ℝ) (L : ℝ≥0) : Prop where105  positive : 0 < L106  differentiable : ∀ i, Differentiable ℝ (U i)107  lipschitz : ∀ i, LipschitzWith L (gradient (U i))
Exact statement as printed in the paper
\begin{restatable}[Lipschitz gradient]{assumption_app}{lipschitzgradientrestatable}\label{assump:lipschitz_grad}
The log-likelihood $\tilde\ell^m(\theta, \phi,z_0):=\log \tilde{p}_{\theta,\phi}(x^m,z_0)$ is differentiable and its gradient 
is $L$-Lipschitz for some $L > 0$, \emph{i.e.} for all $(\theta, \phi, z_0), (\theta',\phi', z_0') \in \Theta \times \Phi \times \sZ$,
\begin{align*}
    &\|\nabla \tilde\ell^m(\theta, \phi, z_0) - \nabla \tilde\ell^m(\theta',\phi', z_0')\| \\
    &\qquad \quad \, \leq L\|(\theta, \phi, z_0) - (\theta', \phi', z_0')\|.
\end{align*}
\end{restatable}

Added regularity — R1–R7

These blue hypotheses are additions to the paper’s green A1–A4. They state sufficient regularity, domain and initialization conditions for the corrected source proofs. They contain no assumed entropy-dissipation identity, desired transport inequality or numerical error bound. The orange NNN assumptions belong only to the later new theory.

Added source regularity — RRR hypothesis

R1 — Admissible density laws and finite energies

Mathematical statement

Use M≥1M\ge1M≥1, actual positive finite normalizers, and the probability posteriors obtained by dividing the supplied tilted density by its integral. Work on the finite-KL energy domain, and require the posterior comparison laws to belong to the chosen finite-second-moment domain. The initial laws must have the regularity used by the proof; arbitrary Dirac initial laws cannot simultaneously have positive smooth densities at time zero. Positive-time smoothing is an alternative when the initial energy is defined by its right limit. Normalization and the variational identity are proved from the densities, rather than added as assumptions.

Added source regularity — RRR hypothesis

R2 — Local domination for differentiation of actual integrals

Mathematical statement

On one common neighbourhood of the time or parameter in question, require measurable positive densities, pointwise density and potential derivatives, finite base energy, and an integrable bound for the differentiated integrand. For normalizers the bound is on e−Uu(z)∥∇uUu(z)∥e^{-U_u(z)}\|\nabla_uU_u(z)\|e−Uu​(z)∥∇u​Uu​(z)∥; for the evolving energy it is on q˙(log⁡q+U+1)+qU˙\dot q(\log q+U+1)+q\dot Uq˙​(logq+U+1)+qU˙. Require the weighted parameter gradient to be integrable. These are ordinary sufficient conditions for differentiating under the integral sign. The potential time derivative is derived by the chain rule, and evidence optimality then proves that the average posterior parameter score is zero.

/-!
# Density free-energy differentiation and the Fokker–Planck equation

The density energy is the actual integral `∫ q (log q + U)`. Its time
derivative follows from pointwise time derivatives and local domination.
The weak Fokker–Planck equation is tested against the chemical potential;
the free-energy dissipation identity is a theorem, never a regularity field.

The classical version below derives the weak identity from the pointwise PDE
and ordinary Lebesgue integration by parts. Its tail assumptions are absolute
integrability of the three products in that integration-by-parts theorem.
-/

open MeasureTheory Filter Set
open scoped Topology

and contain no assertion about the derivative of an integral. -/

parameter-path constructor below derives this final field by the chain rule. -/

# Differentiating the actual evidence and centering posterior scores

The normalizer is the actual integral of `exp (-U)`. Common-neighborhood
domination proves its derivative, and normalization identifies the derivative
of its logarithm with the actual posterior mean score. At an evidence
maximizer the average posterior parameter gradient therefore vanishes.
Neither a zero-score condition nor an evidence derivative is assumed.

  [CompleteSpace A] [MeasurableSpace Z]

integrability and differentiation domination on one common neighborhood. -/


/-- The actual normalizing integral has the derivative obtained by
differentiating its positive density under the integral sign. -/

185theorem sum_posterior_parameter_gradient_eq_zero {M : ℕ} (hM : 0 < M)186    (ν : Measure Z) (U : Fin M → A → Z → ℝ) (a : A)187    (data : ∀ i, LocalNormalizerRegularity ν (U i) a)188    (hmeas : ∀ i, Measurable (fun z ↦ Real.exp (-U i a z)))189    (hZ : ∀ i, 0 < normalizer ν (U i) a)190    (hmax : IsLocalMax (logEvidence ν U) a) :191    ∑ i, (∫ z, gradient (fun b ↦ U i b z) a ∂posterior ν (U i) a) = 0
Added source regularity — RRR hypothesis

R3 — Classical flow equations and integrable spatial tails

Mathematical statement

Use the parameter gradient ODE and the actual classical Fokker–Planck equation ∂tqm=∇ ⁣⋅(qm∇(log⁡qm+Um))\partial_tq^m=\nabla\!\cdot(q^m\nabla(\log q^m+U_m))∂t​qm=∇⋅(qm∇(logqm+Um​)). To integrate by parts, require differentiable flux components and absolute integrability of each component times the test, its derivative times the test, and the component times the test derivative. These are the explicit hypotheses of ordinary Lebesgue integration by parts on the unbounded latent domain. Applying them to the chemical potential proves Fisher integrability and the full de Bruijn identity. Applying them to arbitrary admissible continuity-equation velocities proves the normalized product-gradient pairing. Neither conclusion is assumed.

NoBoundaryFlux · definition and context

Exact shared Lean context
import LatentDiffusion.SourceCalculus
import Mathlib.Analysis.Calculus.LineDeriv.IntegrationByParts
import Mathlib.Analysis.InnerProductSpace.PiL2
import Mathlib.Analysis.InnerProductSpace.Trace
import Mathlib.Analysis.Calculus.Gradient.Basic
import Mathlib.MeasureTheory.Function.L2Space

set_option linter.style.header false

/-!
# Density free-energy differentiation and the Fokker–Planck equation

The density energy is the actual integral `∫ q (log q + U)`. Its time
derivative follows from pointwise time derivatives and local domination.
The weak Fokker–Planck equation is tested against the chemical potential;
the free-energy dissipation identity is a theorem, never a regularity field.

The classical version below derives the weak identity from the pointwise PDE
and ordinary Lebesgue integration by parts. Its tail assumptions are absolute
integrability of the three products in that integration-by-parts theorem.
-/

noncomputable section
open MeasureTheory Filter Set
open scoped Topology

namespace LatentDiffusion.RegularFlowCalculus

/-- Pointwise differentiation of the density energy when both its density and
its potential depend on time. -/

/-- Sufficient local analytic hypotheses for differentiation of the actual
density free energy. These are domination, positivity and pointwise regularity,
and contain no assertion about the derivative of an integral. -/

/-- Domination together with the pointwise potential derivative. The
parameter-path constructor below derives this final field by the chain rule. -/

/-- Dominated differentiation computes the density free-energy derivative. -/

variable {E : Type*} [NormedAddCommGroup E] [InnerProductSpace ℝ E]
  [CompleteSpace E] [MeasurableSpace E]

/-- The chemical potential, which is the density first variation up to an
irrelevant constant on probability-preserving directions. -/

/-- Admissible-test weak Fokker–Planck equation `qdot = div(q ∇(log q+U))`.
All C¹ tests for which both displayed integrands are integrable are allowed.
This is a solution equation, independent of any free-energy calculation. -/

omit [MeasurableSpace E] in

/-- The de Bruijn identity for a regular solution of the weak density equation.
Only pointwise derivatives, domination and the weak PDE are inputs. In
particular, neither an energy derivative nor an energy inequality is assumed. -/

section ClassicalEquation

variable [FiniteDimensional ℝ E] [BorelSpace E]

/-- A component of a vector flux in the standard orthonormal basis. -/

/-- Classical divergence written in an orthonormal basis. -/

omit [CompleteSpace E] [MeasurableSpace E] [BorelSpace E] in

omit [CompleteSpace E] [MeasurableSpace E] [BorelSpace E] in

omit [CompleteSpace E] [MeasurableSpace E] [BorelSpace E] in
/-- The orthonormal-coordinate divergence is the trace of the actual spatial
Fréchet derivative. No trace/divergence identification is assumed. -/

/-- Explicit decay conditions sufficient for spatial integration by parts.
The three products are exactly those in the ordinary Lebesgue theorem;
no integral identity is one of the fields. Schwartz fluxes and tests with
polynomial growth are a standard class satisfying these hypotheses. -/

omit [CompleteSpace E] in

/-- Absolute integrability of the vector flux pairing follows from the
componentwise integration-by-parts hypotheses. -/

omit [CompleteSpace E] in

/-- Lebesgue integration by parts gives the divergence weak equation from
classical spatial derivatives and explicit tail integrability. -/

/-- The transport integration-by-parts identity under the actual density law.
It is derived from Lebesgue integration by parts and the pointwise derivative
of `log q`. This is the entropy-score pairing used by displacement calculus. -/

/-- Both actual law integrals in the transport score identity are absolutely
integrable; the identity does not exploit the total integral's default value. -/

/-- Classical Fokker–Planck flux. Its negative divided by `q` is the
continuity-equation velocity `-∇(log q+U)`. -/

/-- A pointwise Fokker–Planck equation has its expected weak identity whenever
the ordinary integration-by-parts products are integrable. -/

/-- The first variation in a genuine continuity-equation direction. The
velocity field is arbitrary; its pairing with the score is a conclusion of
integration by parts, rather than an assumed Wasserstein derivative. -/

/-- Actual energy differentiation in any classical continuity-equation
direction. This is the integral first-variation formula needed to represent
the source gradient on its normalized product tangent space. -/

/-- The full density de Bruijn identity is proved from the classical PDE.
All added assumptions are local differentiability/domination, spatial C¹
regularity, absolute integrability and the pointwise solution equation. -/

end ClassicalEquation

section ParameterCalculus

variable {A X : Type*} [NormedAddCommGroup A] [InnerProductSpace ℝ A]
  [CompleteSpace A] [MeasurableSpace X]

/-- The actual integral of the parameter gradient under a density. -/

/-- The weighted parameter directional derivative is integrable, and equals
the inner product against the actual integral parameter gradient. -/

/-- Parameter time derivatives used in the energy integral are derived by the
ordinary chain rule. This is also the constructor for the full analytic data;
the domination data themselves need no potential time-derivative assertion. -/

/-- Along parameter gradient descent, the parameter contribution is exactly
minus the squared norm of the actual averaged gradient. -/

end ParameterCalculus

section NormalizedProduct

variable {A : Type*} [NormedAddCommGroup A] [InnerProductSpace ℝ A]
  [CompleteSpace A] [FiniteDimensional ℝ E] [BorelSpace E] {M : ℕ}

/-- Parameter component of the source's gradient: the average of the actual
integral parameter gradients. -/

/-- The actual source density free energy, normalized by the number of data. -/

/-- Riesz pairing with the source's normalized product gradient. There is no
`1/M` in an individual law-gradient component; it occurs in the tangent metric
itself. -/

omit [NormedAddCommGroup E] [InnerProductSpace ℝ E] [CompleteSpace E]
    [FiniteDimensional ℝ E] [BorelSpace E] in

/-- Source gradient representation for the actual density energy and every
admissible parameter/transport tangent. Parameter differentiation comes from
the chain rule and integration; law differentiation comes from the actual
continuity equation and proved spatial integration by parts.

This simultaneously fixes the normalization: the parameter gradient is the
average force, while each law gradient is `∇(log q_i + U_i)`. -/

/-- The squared norm of the source gradient in its normalized product metric,
written using the actual density integrals. -/

omit [FiniteDimensional ℝ E] [BorelSpace E] in
/-- The actual normalized product-gradient norm is nonnegative. -/

/-- Source de Bruijn identity for the full normalized parameter/law system.
The parameter ODE is `pdot=-average ∫q∇_parameter U`; each law satisfies its
classical Fokker–Planck PDE. Integrability of the Fisher integrands is proved
from the spatial tail conditions, alongside the energy derivative.

No entropy derivative, entropy dissipation or convergence bound is assumed. -/

end NormalizedProduct

end LatentDiffusion.RegularFlowCalculus

Added source regularity — RRR hypothesis

R4 — Regular displacement charts and actual optimal transports

Mathematical statement

For the transport arguments, use smooth displacement maps with positive Jacobian eigenvalues, actual pushforward density laws, the density/Jacobian change-of-variables equation, and integrable logarithms and quadratic transport costs. When an exact Wasserstein distance is needed, supply an optimal map by its pushforward and minimality against every genuine coupling. For the geodesic equivalence, require optimal maps between all intermediate laws and endpoint-map uniqueness up to source-law null sets. Its gradient-map version uses an actual convex potential and its gradient certificate. This is explicit regular transport data; arbitrary probability laws are not asserted to possess a smooth positive-Jacobian map. Entropy displacement convexity and its score tangent inequality are proved from the Jacobian formula and spatial integration by parts. No entropy-convexity, first-order transport or log-Sobolev inequality is an assumption in these data.

R5 — Square-integrable characteristic curves for metric bounds

Mathematical statement

Realize the evolving law by an actual square-integrable characteristic curve with its stated time derivative. Require the characteristic velocity to be integrable on finite time intervals. Represent transport to a fixed target by an optimal anchor whose law is that target and whose cost is minimal among all couplings. The law-distance increment and integrated speed bounds are then proved from the characteristic curve and coupling costs. At a crossing of the target, use the upper-right-slope statement; an ordinary distance derivative need not exist there.

R6 — A complete dominated density domain for the limit argument

Mathematical statement

For compactness in the regular density domain, require a complete metric chart with pointwise continuous densities and potentials and a common local integrable envelope for qlog⁡q+qUq\log q+qUqlogq+qU. When this chart carries the source product transport metric, pointwise density continuity is an additional regular-domain requirement; it does not follow from Wasserstein convergence alone. Dominated convergence proves continuity, hence lower semicontinuity, of the actual energy. A Cauchy sequence of flow states whose energies approach the infimum then has an admissible minimizing limit. Completeness is not attributed to the unrestricted subspace of smooth densities.

R7 — Stochastic initialization and uniform moment control

Mathematical statement

Use square-integrable initial clouds, the actual continuous L2L^2L2 Brownian integral equation, Brownian increments independent across their declared particle coordinates and independent of the initial state, and compatible coupled initializations. Initialize the frozen posterior comparison with its actual Gibbs law. The Gibbs stationarity theorem then constructs the stationary frozen reference; independence and the evidence-optimum score identity control its empirical parameter-force fluctuation. Explicitly require one fixed per-copy bound E∥Si−ESi∥2≤V0\mathbb E\|S_i-\mathbb ES_i\|^2\le V_0E∥Si​−ESi​∥2≤V0​, with V0V_0V0​ independent of the particle count, and a uniform normalized initialization radius when quoting a count-independent transient. These are sampling/initialization and moment assumptions in addition to analytic regularity. The solution class is continuous in L2L^2L2 and solves the actual Brownian integral equation; a separate progressively measurable, almost-sure continuous-path realization is not asserted. Numerical errors and their recurrences are proved from these inputs, rather than assumed. Count-independent temporal constants also require a uniform bound on the normalized force at the origin, as well as the state moment bound. For Euler discretization use the explicit additional restriction 0<h,  λh≤1,  hL2≤λ0<h,\;\lambda h\le1,\;hL^2\le\lambda0<h,λh≤1,hL2≤λ.

/-!
# A closed full-batch theorem from an actual frozen posterior equation

The added analytic input is an actual continuous stationary frozen posterior
solution driven by Brownian noise. Its integral equation, initial optimality and
independent posterior scores are explicit. Numerical defects, empirical-force
residual estimates and reference moment bounds are conclusions, not inputs.
The drift constant below is its exact initial second moment, which is finite
because both the initial cloud and the Lipschitz force belong to L².
-/

/-- Extract a parameter block from any finite sum of coordinates. -/





/-- Orthogonal projection onto the latent block. -/





variable {K dθ dz : ℕ}

/-- One actual per-datum parameter score, inserted into the joint cloud. -/


/-- Removing the latent force leaves precisely the empirical parameter score. -/

section Probability
variable {Ω : Type*} [MeasurableSpace Ω] (P : Measure Ω) [IsProbabilityMeasure P]

/-- The frozen reference force is obtained by zeroing only the optimizer drift. -/


/-- Actual square-integrable per-datum scores; finite moments follow from

/-- A Lipschitz observable has exactly the same L² norm on equal input laws. -/

/-- Exact moments of independent centered L² variables, with only the first
order condition on the sum of their means. Individual data means may differ. -/

/-- The original latent Brownian vector is inserted without optimizer noise. -/





/-- Cumulative physical noise: sqrt(2/K) Brownian forcing in scaled latent
coordinates, exactly zero parameter forcing. -/

/-- Explicit physical Brownian root-mean-square coefficient. It simplifies to
sqrt(2 dz) when K>0; its displayed form also covers the empty cloud. -/



/-- Equal laws transfer arbitrary continuous square-integrable observables. -/





/-- Optimizer coordinates of the frozen force vanish as an L² identity. -/

/-- Every physical Brownian input has exactly zero optimizer coordinates. -/

/-- Additional analytic solution assumption: an actual continuous frozen
posterior solution with its literal Brownian integral equation and invariant
cloud law. Invariance is explicitly a probability-law assumption, separate
from smoothness. No desired finite-particle or discretization estimate occurs.
A Gibbs-stationarity bridge below discharges invariance from an initial Gibbs
law and independent Brownian inputs whenever the latent potential is supplied.
-/

variable {F : Cloud.State K dθ dz → Cloud.State K dθ dz} {m : ℝ} {L : ℝ≥0}
  {hF : ForceRegularity F m L}
  {B : (Fin K × Fin dz) → ℝ≥0 → Ω → ℝ}
  {hB : ∀ i, IsPreBrownianReal (B i) P}

/-- The constant optimizer is proved from zero optimizer drift and zero noise. -/

/-- Segment moment and local defect inputs are all constructed from the global
stationary equation. The drift radius is its exact initial L² norm. -/

/-- Exact initial score-variance budget. It is a finite sum of genuine L²
moments, not an assumed bound on a sampling residual. -/

/-- The full-batch discretization converges to the specified optimizer with
finite-cloud and time-step errors derived from the actual posterior equation.
Initialization, finite-particle variance, drift discretization and Brownian
roughness appear separately; there is no numerical-error hypothesis. -/

/-- Physical latent configurations in particle-normalized cloud coordinates. -/

/-- The same physical embedding acting on actual L² random variables. -/




/-- A structural pointwise force identity passes to actual L² force maps.
For the manuscript the latent potential is the sum of frozen datum potentials.
This is an identity of coefficients, not an error bound. -/

/-- Gibbs stationarity discharges the invariant-law field from a genuine
latent Langevin equation, initial Gibbs law, and independent Brownian inputs.
No invariant process law or moment estimate is assumed in this constructor. -/

/-- The cloud-noise coefficient has no particle-number penalty. -/

/-- Extract all scaled latent coordinates. -/




/-- The physical frozen posterior potential, summed over all datum-particle
pairs. Its latent Gibbs measure has the manuscript's unit temperature. -/




/-- Chain rule includes exactly the reciprocal-sqrt(K) scaling. -/

/-- No free coefficient-matching assumption remains: the actual heterogeneous
frozen cloud force is the embedded gradient of the displayed latent potential. -/





/-- Global Picard construction for a Lipschitz force. Finite-horizon Picard
solutions are glued by their proved same-input uniqueness. -/

/-- The frozen posterior Langevin trajectory is constructed from the actual
initial random variable and Brownian path; existence is not a new hypothesis. -/


/-- The manuscript's actual heterogeneous stationary reference, fully
constructed from initial Gibbs data and independent Brownian coordinates. -/

/-- Packing retains exactly the specified deterministic parameter. -/

/-- The constructed reference starts from the supplied posterior coupling. -/

/-- The reference drift RMS is bounded from the Gibbs score theorem itself;
no a priori drift-moment bound is required. -/

end Probability
end LatentDiffusion.RegularStochastic

recursion. All finite-cloud and time-step errors are proved. No local-defect,
reference-existence, stationarity, force-residual or zero-score premise remains.

normalizers, the posterior initialization laws, and Brownian independence.

/-!
# Differentiating the actual evidence and centering posterior scores

The normalizer is the actual integral of `exp (-U)`. Common-neighborhood
domination proves its derivative, and normalization identifies the derivative
of its logarithm with the actual posterior mean score. At an evidence
maximizer the average posterior parameter gradient therefore vanishes.
Neither a zero-score condition nor an evidence derivative is assumed.
-/

noncomputable section
open MeasureTheory Filter Set
open scoped Topology

namespace LatentDiffusion.RegularEvidence

variable {A Z : Type*} [NormedAddCommGroup A] [InnerProductSpace ℝ A]
  [CompleteSpace A] [MeasurableSpace Z]





/-- Added normalizer regularity consists only of ordinary measurability,
integrability and differentiation domination on one common neighborhood. -/


/-- The actual normalizing integral has the derivative obtained by
differentiating its positive density under the integral sign. -/

omit [NormedAddCommGroup A] [InnerProductSpace ℝ A] [CompleteSpace A] in

/-- The posterior mean gradient is an absolutely integrable actual score. -/

/-- Normalizing the actual density normalizes its integral gradient. -/

/-- The logarithm of the actual normalizer has derivative minus the actual
posterior mean parameter gradient. -/



/-- The full evidence derivative is computed from the actual integrals. -/

/-- At an actual evidence maximum the average posterior parameter gradient
vanishes. This discharges the optimizer-centering condition from evidence
optimality and ordinary dominated differentiation. -/


end LatentDiffusion.RegularEvidence

import LatentDiffusion.Density
import LatentDiffusion.Flow
import Mathlib.Topology.Semicontinuity.Basic
import Mathlib.Topology.MetricSpace.Cauchy
import Mathlib.Analysis.SpecialFunctions.Log.Deriv

set_option linter.style.header false

/-!
# Additional source results, on their explicit mathematical domains

These theorems reconstruct elementary steps used in the supplied manuscript.
They do not construct optimal transport plans, identify a Wasserstein metric
derivative, or justify differentiation or integration by parts on an unbounded
domain. Those continuum application steps remain separate obligations.

`cauchy_minimizing_sequence` corrects Supplement `lem:cauchy`: a Cauchy
sequence must also be a minimizing sequence. A complete ambient metric space
and lower semicontinuity then give an actual minimizer.
-/

noncomputable section
open MeasureTheory Set Filter
open scoped Topology

namespace LatentDiffusion.SourceResults

/-- Corrected Supplement `lem:cauchy`: completeness and lower semicontinuity
identify the limit of a Cauchy *minimizing* sequence as a minimizer.
No unrelated Cauchy sequence supplies this conclusion. -/

/-- The scalar derivative used in Supplement `app:lemma_1st_var` includes
the additive constant one. It disappears only on zero-total-mass directions. -/

/-- Constants represent the same first variation on probability tangent
directions. This proves the precise reason the source may omit `+1`. -/

/-- The source's normalized product metric cancels the `1/M` from the
distributional first variation with the inverse metric's `M`.
The positivity of the data count is essential. -/

/-- The first-order scalar consequence of the source's geodesic-convexity
inequality. This step is proved by taking the right derivative; the existence
and calculus of an actual Wasserstein geodesic is not a premise hidden here. -/

/-- The source's Talagrand-type quadratic growth follows directly from strong
geodesic convexity at a minimizer. This proof needs no entropy dissipation.
The application must still establish the displayed convexity inequality for
its actual displacement interpolation and actual metric distance. -/

/-- The actual tilted density in main-text `eq:ptildedef`. -/

/-- The log-density free energy used by the paper, relative to a base measure. -/

/-- Pointwise tilt identity, including zeros of the trial density. -/

/-- Main-text free-energy decomposition after `eq:free-energy`, proved for
the actual base-density integral. Both integrable summands are explicit. -/

/-- Nonnegative KL regularization raises the density free energy. The KL
interpretation of `R` is independent of this integral inequality. -/

/-- Integrability and evidence order follow from a nonnegative integrable
base density and a measurable nonnegative penalty, as used after main-text
`eq:ptildedef`. The tilted integral is not assumed integrable in advance. -/

/-- Taking logs preserves the source's evidence comparison when the tilted
normalizer is positive. Its positivity must be established for the model. -/

/-- Exact finite uniform expectation over the diffusion time index. This is
the arithmetic mean on `Fin K`, so no sampling or asymptotic premise is used. -/

/-- Supplement `app_eq:diffusion_likelihood` and
`app:one_sample_simplified_diffusion`: without inverse-inclusion scaling,
a uniformly selected summand estimates the average, rather than the sum. -/

/-- Corrected unbiased single-time estimator of a *summed* diffusion
objective: multiply the sampled summand by the number of time indices. -/

end LatentDiffusion.SourceResults

/-!
# Additional source results, on their explicit mathematical domains

These theorems reconstruct elementary steps used in the supplied manuscript.
They do not construct optimal transport plans, identify a Wasserstein metric
derivative, or justify differentiation or integration by parts on an unbounded
domain. Those continuum application steps remain separate obligations.

`cauchy_minimizing_sequence` corrects Supplement `lem:cauchy`: a Cauchy
sequence must also be a minimizing sequence. A complete ambient metric space
and lower semicontinuity then give an actual minimizer.
-/

noncomputable section
open MeasureTheory Set Filter
open scoped Topology

namespace LatentDiffusion.SourceResults

/-- Corrected Supplement `lem:cauchy`: completeness and lower semicontinuity
identify the limit of a Cauchy *minimizing* sequence as a minimizer.
No unrelated Cauchy sequence supplies this conclusion. -/

/-- The scalar derivative used in Supplement `app:lemma_1st_var` includes
the additive constant one. It disappears only on zero-total-mass directions. -/

/-- Constants represent the same first variation on probability tangent
directions. This proves the precise reason the source may omit `+1`. -/

/-- The source's normalized product metric cancels the `1/M` from the
distributional first variation with the inverse metric's `M`.
The positivity of the data count is essential. -/

/-- The first-order scalar consequence of the source's geodesic-convexity
inequality. This step is proved by taking the right derivative; the existence
and calculus of an actual Wasserstein geodesic is not a premise hidden here. -/

/-- The source's Talagrand-type quadratic growth follows directly from strong
geodesic convexity at a minimizer. This proof needs no entropy dissipation.
The application must still establish the displayed convexity inequality for
its actual displacement interpolation and actual metric distance. -/

/-- The actual tilted density in main-text `eq:ptildedef`. -/

/-- The log-density free energy used by the paper, relative to a base measure. -/

/-- Pointwise tilt identity, including zeros of the trial density. -/

/-- Main-text free-energy decomposition after `eq:free-energy`, proved for
the actual base-density integral. Both integrable summands are explicit. -/

/-- Nonnegative KL regularization raises the density free energy. The KL
interpretation of `R` is independent of this integral inequality. -/

/-- Integrability and evidence order follow from a nonnegative integrable
base density and a measurable nonnegative penalty, as used after main-text
`eq:ptildedef`. The tilted integral is not assumed integrable in advance. -/

/-- Taking logs preserves the source's evidence comparison when the tilted
normalizer is positive. Its positivity must be established for the model. -/

/-- Exact finite uniform expectation over the diffusion time index. This is
the arithmetic mean on `Fin K`, so no sampling or asymptotic premise is used. -/

/-- Supplement `app_eq:diffusion_likelihood` and
`app:one_sample_simplified_diffusion`: without inverse-inclusion scaling,
a uniformly selected summand estimates the average, rather than the sum. -/

/-- Corrected unbiased single-time estimator of a *summed* diffusion
objective: multiply the sampled summand by the number of time indices. -/

end LatentDiffusion.SourceResults

V1 — Normalized free energy and finite KL domain

Mathematical statement

Let M>0M>0M>0, let ℓ(a)\ell(a)ℓ(a) be the average tilted log evidence, and let πam\pi_a^mπam​ be the actual normalized posterior probability laws. Set

F(a,q)=−ℓ(a)+1M∑m=1MKL(qm∥πam),KL(qm∥πam)<∞.\mathcal F(a,q)=-\ell(a)+\frac1M\sum_{m=1}^M\mathrm{KL}(q^m\|\pi_a^m),\qquad\mathrm{KL}(q^m\|\pi_a^m)<\infty.F(a,q)=−ℓ(a)+M1​m=1∑M​KL(qm∥πam​),KL(qm∥πam​)<∞.

KL here is the actual measure-theoretic divergence. Finite KL is required before conversion to real numbers. The density-normalization result below proves the log-density integral identity under explicit normalization and entropy-integrability conditions. Those conditions are not inferred from pointwise smoothness.

Exact shared Lean context
import Mathlib.InformationTheory.KullbackLeibler.Basic
import Mathlib.MeasureTheory.Measure.ProbabilityMeasure
import Mathlib.Tactic

/-! # The normalized variational problem

The free energy is defined by its canonical normalized form, minus log evidence
plus average actual KL divergence. Admissibility retains finite KL before any
`toReal` conversion. Identifying this definition with a density integral needs
the usual log-integrability and normalization identities; those are not inferred
from pointwise smoothness. The theorem is valid for arbitrary measurable latent
spaces and arbitrary parameter sets, so in particular for tilted latent models.
-/
noncomputable section
open MeasureTheory
open scoped BigOperators ENNReal
namespace LatentDiffusion

variable {A Z : Type*} [MeasurableSpace Z] {M : ℕ}

/-- The tilted log evidence and its normalized posterior at each datum. -/

namespace PosteriorFamily
variable (P : PosteriorFamily A Z M)

/-- Excludes infinite entropy from real arithmetic. -/

/-- The normalized free energy, equal to the log-density definition on its
finite integrability domain. -/





/-- Equality in the variational bound identifies every posterior, using
Gibbs' equality theorem for actual finite measures. -/

/-- Proposition 1, including the unique optimal variational distribution.
No existence of a log-evidence maximizer is assumed or concluded. -/

end PosteriorFamily

/-- The valid zero-tilt comparison requires a true optimum attaining zero
gap. Zero gap only at a tilted optimum is insufficient. -/

/-- A zero-penalty tilted maximizer can fail to maximize the true likelihood.
Both likelihoods and gaps here are exact real numbers on a two-point model. -/

end LatentDiffusion

Density bridge — The actual log-density integral equals KL minus log evidence

Mathematical statement

Let ρ>0\rho>0ρ>0 be measurable and integrable relative to ν\nuν, with Z=∫ρ dν>0Z=\int\rho\,\mathrm d\nu>0Z=∫ρdν>0. Put π=(ρ/Z)ν\pi=(\rho/Z)\nuπ=(ρ/Z)ν. Let r≥0r\ge0r≥0 be measurable and integrable under π\piπ, with ∫r dπ=1\int r\,\mathrm d\pi=1∫rdπ=1 and rlog⁡r∈L1(π)r\log r\in L^1(\pi)rlogr∈L1(π). Set qν=rρ/Zq_\nu=r\rho/Zqν​=rρ/Z and q=qννq=q_\nu\nuq=qν​ν.

∫qνlog⁡ ⁣(qνρ) dν=∫log⁡ ⁣(qνρ) dq=KL(q∥π)−log⁡Z.\int q_\nu\log\!\left(\frac{q_\nu}{\rho}\right)\,\mathrm d\nu=\int\log\!\left(\frac{q_\nu}{\rho}\right)\,\mathrm dq=\mathrm{KL}(q\|\pi)-\log Z.∫qν​log(ρqν​​)dν=∫log(ρqν​​)dq=KL(q∥π)−logZ.

The theorem constructs both actual probability measures, proves that KL is finite, and proves integrability of the log ratio and this identity. It permits the relative density to vanish. The regular variational module additionally realizes every finite-KL trial law by its actual Radon–Nikodym density.

Exact shared Lean context
import LatentDiffusion.Variational
import UnadjustedLangevin.LSI.KLOfDensity

/-!
# The actual log-density integral and the normalized KL free energy

This file proves the normalization bridge rather than assuming the variational
identity. A nonnegative relative density has finite actual KL whenever its
entropy integrand is integrable. An unnormalized positive base density `ρ` with
positive finite normalizer `Z` gives an actual probability posterior `ρ/Z`.
For a normalized relative density `r`, the trial law has actual base density
`rρ/Z`. Its integral of `log ((rρ/Z)/ρ)` is proved to equal `KL - log Z`.
Zero values of `r` are handled on the trial law's full-measure positive support.
-/

noncomputable section
open MeasureTheory
open scoped ENNReal

namespace LatentDiffusion.Density

variable {E : Type*} [MeasurableSpace E]

/-- The actual measure whose density relative to `ν` is the supplied real `r`. -/

/-- Normalization follows from the ordinary integral of the nonnegative density. -/

/-- Points where the relative density vanishes have zero induced probability. -/

/-- Finite actual KL and the shifted logarithm integral follow from a normalized
relative density and an integrable entropy integrand. No KL identity is a premise. -/

/-- The posterior is the actual base measure tilted by `ρ/Z`. -/

/-- An ordinary positive finite normalizer constructs a posterior probability. -/

/-- The trial density relative to the original base measure. -/

/-- Composition of actual density changes gives the claimed base density. -/

/-- The ordinary log ratio agrees on the trial law's actual support. -/

/-- A genuine density-normalization bridge for the source log-density free
energy. The posterior, trial law, finite KL, and integral identity are derived.
The assumptions are density measurability, positivity, normalization and entropy
integrability; the desired variational identity is not assumed. -/

/-- The same bridge in the manuscript's literal base-density integral form:
`∫ f log(f/ρ) dν`, with the actual trial density `f=rρ/Z`. Integrability of this
base-measure expression is also derived, rather than separately assumed. -/

end LatentDiffusion.Density

117theorem density_freeEnergy_eq_kl (ν : Measure E) (ρ r : E → ℝ) (Z : ℝ)118    (hρmeas : Measurable ρ) (hrmeas : Measurable r)119    (hρ : ∀ x, 0 < ρ x) (hr : ∀ x, 0 ≤ r x) (hZ : 0 < Z)120    (hρint : Integrable ρ ν) (hZeq : (∫ x, ρ x ∂ν) = Z)121    (hrint : Integrable r (posteriorMeasure ν ρ Z))122    (hrmass : (∫ x, r x ∂posteriorMeasure ν ρ Z) = 1)123    (hentropy : Integrable (fun x ↦ r x * Real.log (r x)) (posteriorMeasure ν ρ Z)) :124    let π := posteriorMeasure ν ρ Z125    let q := densityMeasure ν (trialDensity ρ r Z)126    IsProbabilityMeasure π ∧ IsProbabilityMeasure q ∧127      InformationTheory.klDiv q π ≠ ⊤ ∧128      Integrable (fun x ↦ Real.log (trialDensity ρ r Z x / ρ x)) q ∧129      (∫ x, Real.log (trialDensity ρ r Z x / ρ x) ∂q) =130        (InformationTheory.klDiv q π).toReal - Real.log Z

Classical flow — Regularity and equations with proved entropy calculus

Mathematical statement

The blue RRR assumptions specify positive density paths, their actual time derivatives, common-neighbourhood integral domination, regular transport charts and integrable spatial tails. The parameter and density equations are

a˙t=−1M∑m∫∇aUm(at,z)qtm(z) dz,∂tqtm=∇ ⁣⋅ ⁣(qtm∇z(log⁡qtm+Um(at,⋅))).\dot a_t=-\frac1M\sum_m\int\nabla_a U_m(a_t,z)q_t^m(z)\,dz,\qquad\partial_tq_t^m=\nabla\!\cdot\!\bigl(q_t^m\nabla_z(\log q_t^m+U_m(a_t,\cdot))\bigr).a˙t​=−M1​m∑​∫∇a​Um​(at​,z)qtm​(z)dz,∂t​qtm​=∇⋅(qtm​∇z​(logqtm​+Um​(at​,⋅))).

ClassicalFlow records these primitive equations and regularity data. The displayed theorems derive the actual energy derivative, normalized extended LSI and exponential energy decay. For the source xLSI-to-Talagrand implication, the separate bare RegularDensityDynamics omits A3 entirely: actual characteristics and coupling anchors derive its metric speed, and xLSI is the sole functional-inequality premise. Dissipation and speed are conclusions of the connected theorem.

import LatentDiffusion.RegularTransportFirstOrder

/-! # Convergence from the classical equations and regular transport

The fields of `ClassicalFlow` are density, differentiability, domination,
transport and boundary integrability data. Energy dissipation and extended
LSI are proved below from those data; neither is a field of the structure.
-/

noncomputable section
set_option linter.unusedSectionVars false

variable {A Z : Type*}
  [NormedAddCommGroup A] [InnerProductSpace ℝ A] [CompleteSpace A]
  [MeasurableSpace A] [BorelSpace A] [SecondCountableTopology A]
  [NormedAddCommGroup Z] [InnerProductSpace ℝ Z] [CompleteSpace Z]
  [MeasurableSpace Z] [BorelSpace Z] [SecondCountableTopology Z]
  [FiniteDimensional ℝ Z] {M d : ℕ}

open RegularTransport RegularFlowCalculus


/-- Gibbs variational lower bound for every positive regular density law.
The proof integrates `log x ≤ x-1`; no KL identity is a premise. -/

namespace RegularDataset

variable {rho : ℝ} {a b : A} (R : DatasetRegularity (Z := Z) M d a b rho)







end RegularDataset

/-- A regular classical solution of the actual normalized parameter ODE and
Fokker–Planck PDE, together with regular transports to the fixed comparison
state. The potential gradients are actual Fréchet gradients, not inequalities.
-/

namespace ClassicalFlow

variable {rho : ℝ} {astar : A} {U : Fin M → A → Z → ℝ}
  (S : ClassicalFlow M d rho astar U)








/-- The terminal coupling law is the actual normalized model posterior;
the Wasserstein target is therefore independent of time. -/





/-- Dissipation is a conclusion of the actual differential equations and
dominated differentiation/spatial integration by parts. -/

/-- Extended LSI is a conclusion of regular transport and joint strong
convexity, with exactly the source normalized Fisher information. -/

/-- Exponential decay of the actual density integral, derived from the
classical equations and joint strong convexity. The endpoint identity only

is proved. Actual square-integrable characteristics and optimal coupling
anchors prove speed in the chart's actual normalized transport metric.
Extended LSI is the sole functional-inequality premise; no strong-convexity
or geodesic-convexity hypothesis is used by this implication.

/-- Actual characteristic kinetic energy equals the actual density Fisher

end CharacteristicRealization

196theorem exists_minimizer_talagrand [CompleteSpace X]197    (Fstar rho : ℝ) (hrho : 0 < rho) (hstar : ∀ x, Fstar ≤ D.energy x)198    (hxLSI : ∀ x, 2 * rho * (D.energy x-Fstar) ≤199      normalizedSlopeSquared volume (fun i ↦ (D.chart i).density x) U (D.parameter x)) :200    ∃ xstar, Tendsto (fun n : ℕ ↦ R.state n) atTop (𝓝 xstar) ∧201      D.energy xstar = Fstar ∧ (∀ x, D.energy xstar ≤ D.energy x) ∧202      ∀ t, 0 ≤ t → rho * dist (R.state t) xstar ^ 2 ≤203        2 * (D.energy (R.state t)-Fstar)

Paper results — all 19 source statements

Each card states the corrected source claim, identifies its RRR hypotheses and precise correction, and shows its Lean theorem. The exact original TeX is expandable for direct comparison.

  1. Variational characterization of the tilted likelihood
  2. Unique tilted optimizer and exponential parameter convergence
  3. Nonasymptotic error of the full-batch Euler scheme
  4. First variations of the free energy
  5. Gradient under the normalized Euclidean–Wasserstein metric
  6. de Bruijn identity for the joint flow
  7. Geodesics in the normalized product space
  8. Strong geodesic convexity of the tilted free energy
  9. First-order lower bound along a transport geodesic
  10. Strong log-concavity implies extended log-Sobolev control
  11. Metric-speed control of distance along the flow
  12. Lower semicontinuity of the tilted energy
  13. A Cauchy flow sequence with optimal energies reaches a minimizer
  14. Extended log-Sobolev control implies distance to the minimizing set
  15. Full product-state exponential convergence
  16. Continuous mean-field solution and empirical-cloud comparison
  17. Uniform finite-particle approximation error

Suppose Assumptions \Cref{assump:model_reg}-\Cref{assump:strong_log_concave} hold, then $\tilde{\ell}$ has a unique maximizer $(\theta_\star, \phi_\star)$ and the flow converges exponentially fast to it: for $\lambda$ independent of $M$ and all $t\geq 0$,

/-!
# The source full-batch theorem for the actual posterior optimizer

This theorem combines the actual normalized density model, its proved unique
variational optimizer, evidence differentiation, a constructed Gibbs Langevin
reference, independent initial posterior scores, and the actual pointwise Euler
recursion. All finite-cloud and time-step errors are proved. No local-defect,
reference-existence, stationarity, force-residual or zero-score premise remains.
The explicit added assumptions are local domination for differentiating the
normalizers, the posterior initialization laws, and Brownian independence.
-/

is the actual uniquely defined variational optimizer, and the left side is
literally the root mean square error of the pointwise full-batch Euler code.
V is the exact sum of initial posterior parameter-score variances, so V/K² is
computed rather than postulated as an empirical-error bound. -/

/-- A primitive per-copy centered second-moment bound gives an explicit budget
linear in the number of copies. It is independent of any empirical error. -/


/-- The corrected paper rate with K=M*N, an arbitrary initial algorithm
state, and a primitive per-copy posterior score variance V₀. The resulting
finite-particle term is exactly 2 sqrt(V₀/(M*N))/m. -/

/-- Dataset potentials repeated once for each of N particles per datum. -/


/-- Replicating data potentials changes neither average evidence nor its
optimizer; K=M*N in the numerical code has the original M-datum target. -/



/-- Connected continuous-time source theorem: the target is the actual unique
variational optimizer and the stationary comparison process is constructed.
Evidence differentiation proves posterior score cancellation internally; no
reference or optimizer-identification premise is supplied. -/

/-- Parameter plus the per-datum empirical transport cost in the manuscript's
normalized product metric. The particle pairing is synchronous in time. -/


/-- The normalized physical particle pairing is exactly the cloud Hilbert
energy; the reciprocal-sqrt(K) scaling loses no coordinate or factor. -/

/-- A genuine indexwise coupling bounds each per-datum empirical W₂ cost.
This holds for every pair of clouds, with no independence requirement. -/



/-- The empirical-product RMS is a genuine integrable expectation and is

/-- The connected source result for the entire normalized coupled state.

/-- Corrected source empirical-cloud endpoint. A single constructed

the same rate as the full normalized cloud coupling. No independent-target

Exact statement as printed in the paper
\begin{theorem}\label{thrm:error-bound}
Suppose that the premise of Theorem~\ref{thm:exp_convg_informal} and \Cref{assump:lipschitz_grad} hold, and that $\mathcal{R}$ has Lipschitz gradients. For all sufficiently small $h>0$, there exists a constant $C_{h,N}$ of order $\mathcal{O}(h^{1/2}+N^{-1/2})$ independent of $T$, a $\rho \in (0, 1)$, and a $C>0$ independent of $(h,N,T)$, such that
$$\mathbb{E}\left[\vert\vert(\theta_T,\phi_T)-(\theta_\star,\phi_\star) \vert\vert^2\right]^{1/2} \leq C_{h,N}+C\rho^T\quad\forall T\in \mathbb{N},$$
where $(\theta_\star,\phi_\star)$ denote $\tilde{\ell}$'s unique maximizer.
\end{theorem}

/-!
# Dominated first variations of the actual density free-energy integral

Source: `papers/Latent_diffusion/supp_aistats.tex:188–199`,
Lemma `app:lemma_1st_var`.

The parameter result differentiates the actual integral, using pointwise
Fréchet derivatives and one integrable domination bound on a common parameter
neighborhood. The density result differentiates the actual integral along
`q + t r`, using positivity and integrable derivative domination on a common
interval. Neither result assumes the desired integral derivative.

These domination/integrability conditions are additional explicit analytic
hypotheses; the paper's A1 does not by itself establish them. The `+1` in the
ordinary entropy derivative disappears on zero-mass density perturbations.
No Wasserstein gradient, PDE integration by parts or flow construction is
claimed by this module.
-/

noncomputable section

open MeasureTheory Filter
open scoped Topology

variable {Z A : Type*} [MeasurableSpace Z]
  [NormedAddCommGroup A] [NormedSpace ℝ A]

/-- The actual base-density free energy with potential `U = -log ρ`. -/

/-- Parameter differentiation in source Lemma `app:lemma_1st_var`, with an
explicit weighted derivative bound that justifies differentiation under the
integral. The density is held fixed. In the source, use
`U(θ,φ,z) = L_D(θ,z) - log p_φ(x|z)` and split its derivative. -/

/-- The ordinary pointwise derivative along an affine density perturbation.
This is used below inside a dominated differentiation theorem. -/

/-- Genuine density-direction differentiation of the source free-energy
integral. Positivity and the domination bound hold on one common neighborhood
of zero, rather than point-dependent neighborhoods. -/

/-- On probability-density tangent directions the constant `+1` vanishes.
The conclusion is the source's density first variation, now for an actual
integral with all dominated-differentiation hypotheses exposed. -/

end LatentDiffusion.SourceCalculus

Exact statement as printed in the paper
\begin{lemma}\label{app:lemma_1st_var}
     Given the free energy of the form in \eqref{eq_app:decomposed_obj}:
\begin{equation}
    \tilde{F}(\theta, \phi, q)  =  \int \mathcal{L}_D(\theta, z) q(z)\dd z - \int \log \left(\frac{p_\phi( x|z)}{q(z)}\right) q(z)\dd z.
\end{equation}
The first variation $\delta \tilde{F}(\theta, \phi, q)=(\delta_q \tilde{F}(\theta, \phi, q), \delta_\theta \tilde{F}(\theta, \phi, q), \delta_\phi \tilde{F}(\theta, \phi, q))$ is given by:
\begin{align}
    \delta_q \tilde{F}(\theta, \phi, q) &= \log \left(\frac{q(z)}{p_\phi( x|z)}\right) + \mathcal{L}_D(\theta, z)\label{eq_app:1st_var_q}   \\
    \delta_\theta \tilde{F}(\theta, \phi, q) &= \int \nabla_\theta \mathcal{L}_D(\theta, z) q(z) \dd z\label{eq_app:1st_var_theta}  \\
    \delta_\phi \tilde{F}(\theta, \phi, q) &= - \int \nabla_\phi \log p_\phi( x|z) q(z) \dd z\label{eq_app:1st_var_phi} 
\end{align}
\end{lemma}

Under the explicit R2–R3 first-variation and continuity-equation regularity, the parameter and density gradients are

∇uF~=1M∑m∫∇uVum dqm,∇qmF~=−∇z ⁣⋅(qm∇z(log⁡qm+Vum)).\nabla_u\widetilde F=\frac1M\sum_m\int\nabla_u V_u^m\,dq^m, \qquad \nabla_{q^m}\widetilde F=-\nabla_z\!\cdot \bigl(q^m\nabla_z(\log q^m+V_u^m)\bigr).∇u​F=M1​m∑​∫∇u​Vum​dqm,∇qm​F=−∇z​⋅(qm∇z​(logqm+Vum​)).

Thus the descent flow has u˙=−M−1∑m∫∇uVum dqm\dot u=-M^{-1}\sum_m\int\nabla_uV_u^m\,dq^mu˙=−M−1∑m​∫∇u​Vum​dqm and ∂tqm=∇z⋅(qm∇zVum)+Δqm\partial_tq^m=\nabla_z\cdot(q^m\nabla_zV_u^m)+\Delta q^m∂t​qm=∇z​⋅(qm∇z​Vum​)+Δqm.

Added assumptions for this result: R1 · R2 · R3.

Correction / required qualification.The inverse metric in each law block contributes MMM, cancelling the objective's 1/M1/M1/M. There is consequently no additional 1/M1/M1/M in the density drift or diffusion. These formulas use the descent loss VVV, avoiding the inconsistent concise-loss sign in main lines 222–226.

Formal scope. For every admissible parameter direction and classical continuity-equation velocity, R2–R3 prove the differential of the actual normalized density energy as its Riesz pairing with the averaged parameter force and each unscaled law score. Thus the density-block factor is derived from the normalized tangent metric.

/-!
# Density free-energy differentiation and the Fokker–Planck equation

The density energy is the actual integral `∫ q (log q + U)`. Its time
derivative follows from pointwise time derivatives and local domination.
The weak Fokker–Planck equation is tested against the chemical potential;
the free-energy dissipation identity is a theorem, never a regularity field.

The classical version below derives the weak identity from the pointwise PDE
and ordinary Lebesgue integration by parts. Its tail assumptions are absolute
integrability of the three products in that integration-by-parts theorem.
-/

noncomputable section

open scoped Topology

and contain no assertion about the derivative of an integral. -/

parameter-path constructor below derives this final field by the chain rule. -/

Exact statement as printed in the paper
\begin{proposition}
    Under the normalized product geometry of \Cref{app:metric}, the gradients of the averaged free energy $\tilde{F}(\theta, \phi, q^{1:M})$ with respect to $(\theta, \phi, q^{1:M})$ are given by:
    \begin{align}
    \nabla_\theta \tilde{F}(\theta, \phi, q^{1:M}) &= \frac{1}{M}\sum_{m=1}^M \int \left[\nabla_{\theta} \mathcal{L}_D(\theta, z)\right] q^m(z) \dd z \\
    \nabla_\phi \tilde{F}(\theta, \phi, q^{1:M}) &= -\frac{1}{M}\sum_{m=1}^M \int \left[\nabla_{\phi} \log p_{\phi}( x^m | z)\right] q^m(z) \dd z \\
    \nabla_{q^m} \tilde{F}(\theta, \phi, q^{1:M}) &=  \nabla_{z} \cdot \left[
        q^m(z) \nabla_{z} \left[
            \log \left(
                \frac{p_{\phi}( x^m|z)}{q^m(z)}
            \right) - \mathcal{L}_D(\theta, z)
        \right]
    \right], \quad \forall m\in[M].
\end{align}
\end{proposition}

Exact statement as printed in the paper
\begin{lemma}[Geodesics on $\mathcal{M}^{1:M}$]\label{lem:geodesic}
    A curve $\gamma(t) : t \in [0, 1] \mapsto \mathcal{M}^{1:M}$ is a geodesic if and only if $\gamma(t) = (\gamma_{\theta}(t), \gamma_\phi (t), \gamma_{q^1}(t), \ldots, \gamma_{q^M}(t))$, where $\gamma_{\theta}$ and $\gamma_\phi$ are geodesics in the Euclidean parameter space and each $\gamma_{q^m}$ is a geodesic in $(\mathcal{P}_2(\sZ), \mathrm{d}_{W_2})$. In particular, if $\gamma(t)$ is a geodesic in $\mathcal{M}^{1:M}$ connecting $(\theta, \phi, q^{1:M})$ and $(\theta', \phi', (q')^{1:M})$ then 
    \begin{align*}
        \gamma_{\theta}(t) &= (1-t)\theta + t\theta', \\
        \gamma_{\phi}(t) &= (1-t)\phi + t\phi', \\
        \gamma_{q^m}(t) &= (h_t)_{\#}\varrho^m, \quad m=1,\ldots,M,
    \end{align*}
    where $\varrho^m$'s are Wasserstein-2 optimal transport plans for $(q^m, (q')^m)$ and $h_t(z,z') = (1-t)z + tz'$. Furthermore, if $q^m$'s have densities with respect to the Lebesgue measure, then we can also write:
    \begin{align*}
        \gamma_{q^m}(t) = ((1-t)\mathrm{id} + t\nabla_z f^m)_{\#} q^m, \quad \forall m \in [M],
    \end{align*}
    for some convex function $f^m$.
\end{lemma}

lem:geodesic_convexity · supp_aistats.tex:548–554

Mathematical statement

Suppose each Um(u,z)=−log⁡ρum(z)U_m(u,z)=-\log\rho_u^m(z)Um​(u,z)=−logρum​(z) is jointly λ\lambdaλ-strongly convex. For a constant-speed product Wasserstein geodesic γs\gamma_sγs​ between states a,ba,ba,b, on a finite, integrable R1/R4 density-energy domain, the corrected result is

F~(γs)≤(1−s)F~(a)+sF~(b)−λ2s(1−s)d(a,b)2,0≤s≤1.\widetilde F(\gamma_s)\le(1-s)\widetilde F(a) +s\widetilde F(b)-\frac\lambda2s(1-s)d(a,b)^2, \qquad 0\le s\le1.F(γs​)≤(1−s)F(a)+sF(b)−2λ​s(1−s)d(a,b)2,0≤s≤1.

The potential term uses joint strong convexity along optimal displacement interpolations; the negative entropy term uses displacement convexity.

Added assumptions for this result: R1 · R4.

Correction / required qualification.The normalized product distance is essential for the constant to remain independent of MMM. The corrected theorem uses finite entropy and integrable potentials along the full displacement interpolation; finite second moments alone do not imply those conditions.

Formal scope. Entropy displacement convexity is proved from the positive Jacobian change-of-variables formula. Joint A3 convexity gives the potential part, and the normalized data average yields the actual product transport inequality on R4. Entropy convexity itself is not an assumed bridge.

/-!
# Regular displacement transport for the latent free energy

The extra hypotheses below are classical transport regularity data: a
pushforward by a measurable interpolation, positive densities, positive
eigenvalues of its Jacobian, the density/Jacobian change of variables formula,
and integrable logarithms and quadratic costs.  No convexity, first order
transport inequality, log Sobolev inequality, or Talagrand inequality is included
in these data.  The Jacobian may have arbitrary eigenvectors depending on the
latent variable, so this does not restrict to independent coordinates.

The transport distance used throughout is the infimum over actual probability
couplings defined in `ULA.Coupling`.  In particular, finite transport costs are
proved before converting any extended nonnegative real to a real number.
-/

\begin{lemma}[Geodesic convexity of $\tilde{F}$]\label{lem:geodesic_convexity}
    Under Assumption~\Cref{assump:strong_log_concave}, the tilted free energy $\tilde{F}(\theta, \phi, q^{1:M})$ is $\lambda$-geodesically convex on $\mathcal{M}^{1:M}$, that is, for any pair $(\theta, \phi, q^{1:M})$ and $(\theta', \phi', (q')^{1:M})$ in $\mathcal{M}^{1:M}$ and any geodesic $\gamma(t)$ connecting them, we have:
    \begin{align*}
        \tilde{F}(\gamma(t)) &\leq (1-t)\tilde{F}(\theta, \phi, q^{1:M}) + t\tilde{F}(\theta', \phi', (q')^{1:M}) 
        - \frac{\lambda t(1-t)}{2}\mathsf{d}_{\mathcal{M}^{1:M}}((\theta, \phi, q^{1:M}), (\theta', \phi', (q')^{1:M}))^2.
    \end{align*}
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:lower_deriv}
    Let $\gamma(t)$ be a geodesic in $\mathcal{M}^{1:M,1}$ connecting $(\theta, \phi, q^{1:M})$ and $(\theta', \phi', (q')^{1:M})$. Then we have:
    \begin{align*}
        \liminf_{t \to 0^+} \frac{\tilde{F}(\gamma(t)) - \tilde{F}(\gamma(0))}{t} &\geq \frac{1}{M} \sum_{m=1}^M \left\langle \dot{\gamma}_{q^m}(0), \nabla_{q^m} \tilde{F}(\theta, \phi, q^{m}) \right\rangle_{q^m} + \langle

        \rangle
    \end{align*}
\end{lemma}

Proved corrected statement under the explicitly added blue RRR regularity hypotheses. The precise corrections to the printed source are stated below.

Mathematical statement

Under the R3 equations and R5 characteristic realization, the actual normalized product-distance upper-right slope to every fixed state bbb is at most I(at)\sqrt{I(a_t)}I(at​)​. With integrable characteristic velocities, the proved integrated estimate is, for s≤ts\le ts≤t,

∣d(at,b)−d(as,b)∣≤∫stI(ar) dr.|d(a_t,b)-d(a_s,b)|\le\int_s^t\sqrt{I(a_r)}\,dr.∣d(at​,b)−d(as​,b)∣≤∫st​I(ar​)​dr.

Added assumptions for this result: R3 · R5.

Correction / required qualification.The source says the ordinary derivative exists and satisfies the bound at every positive time. Even a smooth Euclidean path can have a corner in its distance to a fixed point when it crosses that point. An almost-everywhere metric-derivative statement, or an upper-Dini-derivative formulation, supplies the integrated estimate actually needed by the proof.

Formal scope. For actual square-integrable characteristic curves and target laws under R5, the infimum over genuine coupling costs gives the distance-increment bound. The corrected upper-right-slope and integrated-speed statements are proved. They cover crossing times where the printed ordinary derivative need not exist.

lem:lower_semi_continuous · supp_aistats.tex:656–658

Proved corrected statement under the explicitly added blue RRR regularity hypotheses. The precise corrections to the printed source are stated below.

Mathematical statement

On the R6 density chart equipped with the actual normalized product transport metric, assume pointwise continuous densities and potentials and a common local integrable envelope for qlog⁡q+qUq\log q+qUqlogq+qU. The actual normalized energy

F~(x)=1M∑m∫qxm(z)[log⁡qxm(z)+Um(ux,z)] dz\widetilde F(x)=\frac1M\sum_m\int q_x^m(z) [\log q_x^m(z)+U_m(u_x,z)]\,dzF(x)=M1​m∑​∫qxm​(z)[logqxm​(z)+Um​(ux​,z)]dz

is continuous, hence lower semicontinuous. In particular, for xn→xx_n\to xxn​→x in this chart,

F~(xn)⟶F~(x),F~(x)≤lim inf⁡nF~(xn).\widetilde F(x_n)\longrightarrow\widetilde F(x),\qquad \widetilde F(x)\le\liminf_n\widetilde F(x_n).F(xn​)⟶F(x),F(x)≤nliminf​F(xn​).

Dominated convergence proves this statement on the explicitly identified probability-law domain.

Added assumptions for this result: R1 · R6.

Correction / required qualification.Joint continuity of RRR is used at supplement line 665 but is not an explicit displayed assumption. The corrected proof instead states the sufficient R6 pointwise density/potential continuity and local integrable domination for the total energy. The limiting argument uses a complete admissible R6 domain; differentiable densities alone do not form a complete Wasserstein space.

Formal scope. On the complete regular density domain specified by R6, pointwise density/potential continuity and a local integrable energy envelope prove continuity of the actual density energy by dominated convergence, hence its lower semicontinuity. Pointwise density continuity is an explicit added domain condition, not an inference from Wasserstein convergence alone.

namespace LatentDiffusion.RegularTalagrand


/-- At zero energy the nonnegative dissipating energy stays zero to the right,
so its square root has right derivative zero even though sqrt is singular. -/

/-- Extended LSI controls the square-root energy's dissipation by the metric
speed. The zero-energy case is handled by the preceding right-constancy proof. -/

/-- Adding a differentiable scalar correction to an upper-right slope bound
preserves the bound. The result is stronger than the liminf input to Grönwall. -/

/-- Finite remaining flow length: the product of sqrt(2 rho) with any distance
increment is paid for by the drop of twice the square-root energy. -/



/-- Extended LSI implies the corrected Talagrand conclusion by the full
flow-length argument on a complete metric energy domain. No minimizer or
geodesic convexity is an input: a minimizing limit is constructed.

In the latent-density application, dissipation is supplied by
`normalized_product_deBruijn` and upper slopes by the characteristic/coupling
theorem. Lower semicontinuity is supplied by the dominated density chart. -/

end LatentDiffusion.RegularTalagrand

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:cauchy}
    Denote $\mathcal{M}_\star := \arg\min_{(\theta, \phi, q^{1:M}) \in \mathcal{M}^{1:M}} \tilde{F}(\theta, \phi, q^{1:M})$ as the set of minimizers of $\tilde{F}$ and $\tilde{F}_\star := \inf_{(\theta, \phi, q^{1:M}) \in \mathcal{M}^{1:M}} \tilde{F}(\theta, \phi, q^{1:M})$ as the optimal value. Under the extended log-Sobolev inequality, for a Cauchy sequence $\{(\theta_n, \phi_n, q_n^{1:M})\}_{n\in \mathbb{N}}$ in $\mathcal{M}^{1:M,1}$, there exists an increasing sequence of $t_n \to +\infty$ such that:
    \begin{equation*}
        (\theta_{t_n}, \phi_{t_n}, q_{t_n}^{1:M}) \to (\theta_\star, \phi_\star, q_\star^{1:M}) \in \mathcal{M}_\star, \quad \text{as} \ n \to +\infty,
    \end{equation*}
    for some $(\theta_\star, \phi_\star, q_\star^{1:M}) \in \mathcal{M}_\star$ in the topology induced by $\mathsf{d}_{\mathcal{M}^{1:M}}$ on $\mathcal{M}^{1:M}$.
\end{lemma}

Exact statement as printed in the paper
\begin{theorem}\label{thm:exp_convg_appendix}
    Suppose Assumptions~\Cref{assump:model_reg}-\Cref{assump:strong_log_concave} are satisfied. Then, $\tilde{\ell}$ has a unique maximizer $(\theta_\star, \phi_\star)$ and the flow converges exponentially fast to it: for some $\lambda>0$ independent of $M$, 
\begin{equation}\label{eq:app_thm_exp}
        \mathsf{d}_{\mathcal{M}^{1:M}}((\theta_t,\phi_t,q_t^{1:M}),(\theta_\star,\phi_\star,q_{\star}^{1:M}))
        \leq
        \sqrt{\frac{2[\tilde{F}(\theta_t, \phi_t, q_t^{1:M}) - \tilde{F}_\star]}{\lambda}}
        \leq
        \sqrt{\frac{2[\tilde{F}(\theta_0, \phi_0, q_0^{1:M})-\tilde{F}_\star]}{\lambda}}e^{-\lambda t}, \quad \forall t>0;
\end{equation}
where $\tilde{F}_\star:=\inf_{(\theta,\phi,q^{1:M})\in \mathcal{M}^{1:M}}\tilde{F}(\theta,\phi,q^{1:M})$ and $\vert\vert\cdot\vert\vert$ denotes the Euclidean norm.
\end{theorem}

# Actual nonstationary mean-field, spatial, and temporal comparisons

All drifts are computed from the original heterogeneous pair potentials. The
added moment assumptions concern actual reference forces, and the independence
assumptions concern the supplied independent posterior/reference copies.
Neither a propagation-of-chaos estimate nor a numerical error is a premise.
-/

/-- Actual McKean mean-field force: expected parameter score, pointwise latent
scores. The force is globally Lipschitz, proved from pointwise regularity. -/


/-- Constructed global continuous L² mean-field solution. Existence is derived
by Picard from the original smooth drift and Brownian input. -/

/-- The exact empirical force left by mean-field averaging is the average of
centered per-datum parameter scores. -/

/-- Centering a finite sum is exactly the finite sum of centered variables. -/

/-- Independent heterogeneous mean-field scores give the explicit empirical
force scale from their primitive centered second moments. -/

/-- Nonstationary spatial discretization: independent reference scores and
one-copy centered second moments imply the actual particle/mean-field error.
The bound is uniform at each fixed time; it does not put a time supremum inside
an expectation. The interacting particle solution is constructed by Picard. -/

/-- Primitive actual state moments imply the force-moment input used by Euler
consistency. A force-radius or discretization-error bound is not assumed. -/

/-- Actual nonstationary time discretization from a uniform second-moment
condition on the continuous particle states. The supplied initial state is
arbitrary, the Brownian increments match exactly, and the local defect is
proved from the original integral equation. -/



/-- Averaging is invisible when paired against a deterministic parameter
block. This is the orthogonality identity that proves mean-field contraction. -/

/-- Strong monotonicity of the actual mean-field force on deterministic
parameter states is inherited from the original pair potentials. -/

/-- A mean-field force has a deterministic parameter block equal to the true
expected parameter force. -/


/-- Every actual mean-field solution has deterministic parameter trajectories;
this follows from the equation rather than being imposed on the solution. -/

/-- Actual nonstationary mean-field solutions driven by the same Brownian
input contract exponentially. Joint strong convexity supplies the energy
inequality, and deterministic parameters are the only subspace condition. -/

/-- Equal state laws give equal actual posterior score means. -/

/-- At a zero total posterior score, the computed mean-field drift is exactly
the frozen posterior drift. Individual per-datum score means need not vanish. -/

/-- A constructed stationary posterior reference is also an actual mean-field
solution. Posterior optimality cancels the expected optimizer drift. -/

/-- The actual mean-field optimizer converges to the posterior evidence
optimizer. The initial coupling and parameter are arbitrary; no convergence
estimate is assumed. -/

/-!
# The source full-batch theorem for the actual posterior optimizer

This theorem combines the actual normalized density model, its proved unique
variational optimizer, evidence differentiation, a constructed Gibbs Langevin
reference, independent initial posterior scores, and the actual pointwise Euler
recursion. All finite-cloud and time-step errors are proved. No local-defect,
reference-existence, stationarity, force-residual or zero-score premise remains.
The explicit added assumptions are local domination for differentiating the
normalizers, the posterior initialization laws, and Brownian independence.
-/

/-- Actual physical Brownian increments in particle-normalized coordinates. -/

/-- The corrected source theorem with K=M*N datum-particle pairs. The target
is the actual uniquely defined variational optimizer, and the left side is
literally the root mean square error of the pointwise full-batch Euler code.
V is the exact sum of initial posterior parameter-score variances, so V/K² is
computed rather than postulated as an empirical-error bound. -/

/-- A primitive per-copy centered second-moment bound gives an explicit budget
linear in the number of copies. It is independent of any empirical error. -/


/-- The corrected paper rate with K=M*N, an arbitrary initial algorithm
state, and a primitive per-copy posterior score variance V₀. The resulting
finite-particle term is exactly 2 sqrt(V₀/(M*N))/m. -/

/-- Replicating data potentials changes neither average evidence nor its
optimizer; K=M*N in the numerical code has the original M-datum target. -/



/-- Connected continuous-time source theorem: the target is the actual unique
variational optimizer and the stationary comparison process is constructed.
Evidence differentiation proves posterior score cancellation internally; no
reference or optimizer-identification premise is supplied. -/

/-- Parameter plus the per-datum empirical transport cost in the manuscript's
normalized product metric. The particle pairing is synchronous in time. -/


/-- The normalized physical particle pairing is exactly the cloud Hilbert
energy; the reciprocal-sqrt(K) scaling loses no coordinate or factor. -/

/-- A genuine indexwise coupling bounds each per-datum empirical W₂ cost.
This holds for every pair of clouds, with no independence requirement. -/



/-- The empirical-product RMS is a genuine integrable expectation and is
bounded by the normalized L² cloud distance. No optimal-coupling identity or
transport measurability assumption is supplied. -/


/-- The connected source result for the entire normalized coupled state.
The returned reference has the actual optimizer and actual posterior laws at
every time; full-state contraction is proved before taking any projection. -/

/-- Corrected source empirical-cloud endpoint. A single constructed
synchronous posterior reference carries all times. The true per-datum
empirical W₂ statistic is measurable and integrable, and its RMS contracts at
the same rate as the full normalized cloud coupling. No independent-target
W₂ identity, fixed-time optimality or empirical-error estimate is assumed. -/

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:cont-time-convg}
    Under Assumptions~\Cref{assump:model_reg}, \Cref{assump:strong_log_concave}, and \Cref{assump:lipschitz_grad}, the system of SDEs in~\eqref{eq:app-cont-theta-ode}-\eqref{eq:app-cont-z-sde} admits a unique strong solution $(\tilde\theta_t, Z_t^{1:M,1:N})_{t \geq 0}$ and the solution satisfies
    \begin{equation*}
        \mathsf{d}_{\mathcal{M}^{1:M}}((\tilde\theta_t, Q_t^{1:M,N}), (\tilde\theta_\star, Q_\star^{1:M,N})) \leq C e^{-\lambda t}, \quad \forall t>0,
    \end{equation*}
    where $C>0$ is a constant independent of $N$ and $t$, and we defined the empirical distributions to $q_t^m$ and $q_\star^m$ as $Q_t^{m,N}:=N^{-1}\sum_{n=1}^N \delta_{Z_t^{m,n}}$ and $Q_\star^{m,N}:=N^{-1}\sum_{n=1}^N \delta_{Z_\star^{m,n}}$ respectively, where $Z_\star^{m,n}$ are i.i.d. samples from $\tilde\pi_{\tilde\theta_\star}$ (cf. Remark~\ref{remark:star_notation}).
\end{lemma}
Paper assumption / source result

Uniform finite-particle approximation error
