by Picard from the original smooth drift and Brownian input. -/

/-- The exact empirical force left by mean-field averaging is the average of
centered per-datum parameter scores. -/

/-- Centering a finite sum is exactly the finite sum of centered variables. -/

/-- Independent heterogeneous mean-field scores give the explicit empirical
force scale from their primitive centered second moments. -/

/-- Nonstationary spatial discretization: independent reference scores and
one-copy centered second moments imply the actual particle/mean-field error.
The bound is uniform at each fixed time; it does not put a time supremum inside
an expectation. The interacting particle solution is constructed by Picard. -/

/-- Primitive actual state moments imply the force-moment input used by Euler
consistency. A force-radius or discretization-error bound is not assumed. -/

/-- Actual nonstationary time discretization from a uniform second-moment
condition on the continuous particle states. The supplied initial state is
arbitrary, the Brownian increments match exactly, and the local defect is
proved from the original integral equation. -/



/-- Averaging is invisible when paired against a deterministic parameter
block. This is the orthogonality identity that proves mean-field contraction. -/

/-- Strong monotonicity of the actual mean-field force on deterministic
parameter states is inherited from the original pair potentials. -/

/-- A mean-field force has a deterministic parameter block equal to the true
expected parameter force. -/


/-- Every actual mean-field solution has deterministic parameter trajectories;
this follows from the equation rather than being imposed on the solution. -/

/-- Actual nonstationary mean-field solutions driven by the same Brownian
input contract exponentially. Joint strong convexity supplies the energy
inequality, and deterministic parameters are the only subspace condition. -/

/-- Equal state laws give equal actual posterior score means. -/

/-- At a zero total posterior score, the computed mean-field drift is exactly
the frozen posterior drift. Individual per-datum score means need not vanish. -/

/-- A constructed stationary posterior reference is also an actual mean-field
solution. Posterior optimality cancels the expected optimizer drift. -/

/-- The actual mean-field optimizer converges to the posterior evidence
optimizer. The initial coupling and parameter are arbitrary; no convergence
estimate is assumed. -/

Exact statement as printed in the paper
\begin{lemma}[Spatial Discretization Error]\label{lem:spatial_discretization}
    Suppose Assumptions~\Cref{assump:strong_log_concave} and~\Cref{assump:lipschitz_grad} hold. Then the following system of SDEs:
    \begin{align}
        \dd \tilde\theta_t^N &= \frac{1}{MN} \sum_{m=1}^{M} \sum_{n=1}^N \nabla_{\tilde\theta} \tilde{\ell}^m(\tilde\theta_t^N, \bar{Z}_t^{m,n}) \, \dd t \label{eq_app:spatial1} \\
        \dd \bar{Z}_t^{m,n} &= \nabla_{z} \tilde{\ell}^m(\tilde\theta_t^N, \bar{Z}_t^{m,n}) \, \dd t + \sqrt{2} \, \dd W_t^{m,n}, \quad (m,n)\in[M]\times [N], \label{eq_app:spatial3}
    \end{align}
    has a strong solution $(\tilde\theta_t^N, \bar{Z}_t^{1:M, 1:N})_{t \geq 0}$. Furthermore, there exists a constant $C(N)>0$ of order $\mathcal{O}(N^{-1/2})$ independent of $t$ and $M$, such that:
    \begin{equation*}
        \mathsf{d}_{\mathcal{M}^{1:M}}((\tilde\theta_t^N, \bar{Q}_t^{1:M, N}), (\tilde\theta_t, Q_t^{1:M,N})) \leq C(N), \quad \forall t>0,
    \end{equation*}
    where $\bar{Q}_t^{m, N}:=N^{-1}\sum_{n=1}^N \delta_{\bar{Z}_t^{m,n}}$ for each $m\in [M]$ and $Q_t^{m,N}$ is defined as in Lemma~\ref{lem:cont-time-convg}.
\end{lemma}
Paper assumption / source result

Uniform Euler–Maruyama time-discretization error

\begin{lemma}[Temporal Discretization Error]\label{lem:temporal_discretization}
    Suppose Assumptions~\Cref{assump:strong_log_concave} and~\Cref{assump:lipschitz_grad} hold. Then for the following Euler-Maruyama scheme for the SDEs in \eqref{eq_app:spatial1}-\eqref{eq_app:spatial3}:
    \begin{align}
        \tilde\theta_{k+1}^{N,h} &= \tilde\theta_k^{N,h} + \frac{h}{MN} \sum_{m=1}^{M}\sum_{n=1}^N \nabla_{\tilde\theta} \tilde{\ell}(\tilde\theta_k^{N,h}, \bar{Z}_k^{m,n,N,h}) \label{eq_app:temp1} \\
        \bar{Z}_{k+1}^{m,n,N,h} &= \bar{Z}_k^{m,n,N,h} + h \nabla_{z} \tilde{\ell}(\tilde\theta_k^{N,h}, \bar{Z}_k^{m,n,N,h}) + \sqrt{2h} W_k^n, \quad (m,n) \in [M] \times [N], \label{eq_app:temp3}
    \end{align}
    we have for $h \leq {1}/({\lambda+L})$ with $\lambda$ being the strong concavity constant in Assumption~\Cref{assump:strong_log_concave} and $L$ being the Lipschitz constant in \Cref{assump:lipschitz_grad}, there exists a constant $C(h)>0$ independent of $k$ and $N$ of order $\mathcal{O}(h^{1/2})$,
    such that:
    \begin{equation*}
        \mathsf{d}_{\mathcal{M}^{1:M}}((\tilde\theta_k^{N,h}, \bar{Q}_k^{1:M,N,h}), (\tilde\theta_{kh}^N, \bar{Q}_{kh}^{1:M,N})) \leq \sqrt{h}C(h), \quad \forall k \in \mathbb{N},
    \end{equation*}
\end{lemma}

Exact statement as printed in the paper
\begin{theorem}\label{thrm_app:error-bound}
Suppose that the premise of Theorem~\ref{thm:exp_convg_informal} and \Cref{assump:lipschitz_grad} hold, and that $\mathcal{R}$ has Lipschitz gradients. For all sufficiently small $h>0$, there exists an $\mathcal{O}(h^{1/2}+N^{-1/2})$ constant $C_{h,N}$ independent of $T$, a $\rho \in (0, 1)$, and a $C>0$ independent of $(h,N,T)$, such that
$$\mathbb{E}\left[\vert\vert\tilde\theta_T-\tilde\theta_\star \vert\vert^2\right]^{1/2} \leq C_{h,N}+C\rho^T\quad\forall T\in \mathbb{N},$$
where $\tilde\theta_\star$ denotes $\tilde{\ell}$'s unique maximizer.
\end{theorem}

Corrections to the paper’s formulas and arguments

Each correction names the exact local source location. An algebraic repair and a completed proof of the corresponding flow or algorithm are separate claims.

Universal time-zero density regularity is impossible

assump:solution_reg · main_aistats.tex:151–154 · eq:multi_datapoint_prodmetric · supp_aistats.tex:436–455

The literal time-zero premise is refuted in Lean; R1 states the corrected admissible initial domain.

Mathematical statement
A2 includes every finite-second-moment initial law and requires a smooth density at t=0t=0t=0. A Dirac law has finite second moment but cannot have a density relative to nonatomic Lebesgue measure. Restrict the initial class to the required smooth densities, or require smoothing only for t>0t>0t>0 and continuity in W2W_2W2​ at zero. Merely restricting to absolutely continuous laws still permits discontinuous initial densities. The Dirac obstruction is proved. Existence is proved for the particle and mean-field equations in the continuous L2L^2L2 Brownian integral solution class under R7. The corrected density calculus and decay estimates apply to every classical solution in the explicitly regular class R1–R4; existence of such a classical density solution is not constructed.

/-!
# The literal time-zero solution assumption has an obstruction

An arbitrary finite-second-moment initial law includes a Dirac measure. Such a
law cannot have a density relative to a reference measure that assigns zero mass
to the corresponding singleton. This argument needs no PDE or positivity
assumption. In particular it applies to Lebesgue measure in positive dimension.
-/

noncomputable section
open MeasureTheory Set

namespace LatentDiffusion.SourceObstruction

variable {P Z : Type*} [NormedAddCommGroup P] [NormedSpace ℝ P]
  [NormedAddCommGroup Z] [NormedSpace ℝ Z]
  [MeasurableSpace Z] [MeasurableSingletonClass Z]

/-- The source's universal solution regularity is impossible whenever the
reference measure has even one null singleton. The initial law is an actual
finite-second-moment Dirac probability measure. -/

/-- Atomless reference measures, including positive-dimensional Lebesgue
measures, therefore rule out the literal source premise. -/

end LatentDiffusion.SourceObstruction

Corrected source claim

Zero tilt at the tilted optimum does not identify the original optimum

discussion following prop:ftildemins · main_aistats.tex:107–110

Counterexample and sufficient comparator proved in Lean

Mathematical statement
The pointwise comparison ℓ~≤ℓ\widetilde\ell\le\ellℓ≤ℓ and equality at a tilted maximizer do not imply that this point maximizes ℓ\ellℓ. On two points take log likelihoods (0,1)(0,1)(0,1) and nonnegative gaps (0,2)(0,2)(0,2): the tilted objective (0,−1)(0,-1)(0,−1) is maximized at the zero-gap point, but the original objective is maximized at the other point. A sufficient corrected condition is that an original-objective maximizer has zero gap; then every tilted maximizer attains the original optimal value. Uniform zero penalty across the whole model also suffices.

/-! # The normalized variational problem

The free energy is defined by its canonical normalized form, minus log evidence
plus average actual KL divergence. Admissibility retains finite KL before any
`toReal` conversion. Identifying this definition with a density integral needs
the usual log-integrability and normalization identities; those are not inferred
from pointwise smoothness. The theorem is valid for arbitrary measurable latent
spaces and arbitrary parameter sets, so in particular for tilted latent models.
-/

Mathematical statement
Let p=B/Mp=B/Mp=B/M. The selected gradient has amplitude h/ph/ph/p, so its average drift has the full rate, while every particle receives noise variance 2hp2hp2hp, rather than 2h2h2h. For U(x)=ax2/2U(x)=ax^2/2U(x)=ax2/2, direct Gaussian integration gives E[Xk+12∣Xk=x]=(1−2ah+a2h2/p)x2+2hp\mathbb E[X_{k+1}^2\mid X_k=x]=(1-2ah+a^2h^2/p)x^2+2hpE[Xk+12​∣Xk​=x]=(1−2ah+a2h2/p)x2+2hp. When its denominator is positive, the fixed second moment is p/[a(1−ah/(2p))]p/[a(1-ah/(2p))]p/[a(1−ah/(2p))]. For p=1/2,a=1,h=1/4p=1/2,a=1,h=1/4p=1/2,a=1,h=1/4, target second moment 111 becomes 7/87/87/8 in one step and the fixed moment is 2/32/32/3. Two checked corrections are full noise 2h\sqrt{2h}2h​ with the inverse-inclusion drift, or a random scan that applies uninflated drift and full noise only to selected particles. Their finite-step variances differ; these are scalar moment results, not a general invariant-law theorem for nonlinear IPLD.

/-!
# Exact mini-batch noise and temperature audit

consistency. A force-radius or discretization-error bound is not assumed. -/

condition on the continuous particle states. The supplied initial state is
arbitrary, the Brownian increments match exactly, and the local defect is
proved from the original integral equation. -/



/-- Averaging is invisible when paired against a deterministic parameter
block. This is the orthogonality identity that proves mean-field contraction. -/

/-- Strong monotonicity of the actual mean-field force on deterministic
parameter states is inherited from the original pair potentials. -/

/-- A mean-field force has a deterministic parameter block equal to the true
expected parameter force. -/


/-- Every actual mean-field solution has deterministic parameter trajectories;
this follows from the equation rather than being imposed on the solution. -/

/-- Actual nonstationary mean-field solutions driven by the same Brownian
input contract exponentially. Joint strong convexity supplies the energy

/-- Equal state laws give equal actual posterior score means. -/

/-- At a zero total posterior score, the computed mean-field drift is exactly

/-- A constructed stationary posterior reference is also an actual mean-field
solution. Posterior optimality cancels the expected optimizer drift. -/

/-- The actual mean-field optimizer converges to the posterior evidence
optimizer. The initial coupling and parameter are arbitrary; no convergence
estimate is assumed. -/

/-!
# Density free-energy differentiation and the Fokker–Planck equation

The density energy is the actual integral `∫ q (log q + U)`. Its time
derivative follows from pointwise time derivatives and local domination.
The weak Fokker–Planck equation is tested against the chemical potential;
the free-energy dissipation identity is a theorem, never a regularity field.

The classical version below derives the weak identity from the pointwise PDE
and ordinary Lebesgue integration by parts. Its tail assumptions are absolute
integrability of the three products in that integration-by-parts theorem.
-/

/-!
# Density free-energy differentiation and the Fokker–Planck equation

The density energy is the actual integral `∫ q (log q + U)`. Its time
derivative follows from pointwise time derivatives and local domination.
The weak Fokker–Planck equation is tested against the chemical potential;
the free-energy dissipation identity is a theorem, never a regularity field.

The classical version below derives the weak identity from the pointwise PDE
and ordinary Lebesgue integration by parts. Its tail assumptions are absolute
integrability of the three products in that integration-by-parts theorem.
-/

/-!
# Additional source results, on their explicit mathematical domains

These theorems reconstruct elementary steps used in the supplied manuscript.
They do not construct optimal transport plans, identify a Wasserstein metric
derivative, or justify differentiation or integration by parts on an unbounded
domain. Those continuum application steps remain separate obligations.

`cauchy_minimizing_sequence` corrects Supplement `lem:cauchy`: a Cauchy
sequence must also be a minimizing sequence. A complete ambient metric space
and lower semicontinuity then give an actual minimizer.
-/

namespace LatentDiffusion.SourceResults

/-- Corrected Supplement `lem:cauchy`: completeness and lower semicontinuity
identify the limit of a Cauchy *minimizing* sequence as a minimizer.
No unrelated Cauchy sequence supplies this conclusion. -/

/-- The scalar derivative used in Supplement `app:lemma_1st_var` includes
the additive constant one. It disappears only on zero-total-mass directions. -/

/-- Constants represent the same first variation on probability tangent
directions. This proves the precise reason the source may omit `+1`. -/

/-- The source's normalized product metric cancels the `1/M` from the
distributional first variation with the inverse metric's `M`.
The positivity of the data count is essential. -/

/-- The first-order scalar consequence of the source's geodesic-convexity
inequality. This step is proved by taking the right derivative; the existence
and calculus of an actual Wasserstein geodesic is not a premise hidden here. -/

/-- The source's Talagrand-type quadratic growth follows directly from strong
geodesic convexity at a minimizer. This proof needs no entropy dissipation.
The application must still establish the displayed convexity inequality for
its actual displacement interpolation and actual metric distance. -/

/-- The actual tilted density in main-text `eq:ptildedef`. -/

/-- The log-density free energy used by the paper, relative to a base measure. -/

/-- Pointwise tilt identity, including zeros of the trial density. -/

/-- Main-text free-energy decomposition after `eq:free-energy`, proved for
the actual base-density integral. Both integrable summands are explicit. -/

/-- Nonnegative KL regularization raises the density free energy. The KL
interpretation of `R` is independent of this integral inequality. -/

/-- Integrability and evidence order follow from a nonnegative integrable
base density and a measurable nonnegative penalty, as used after main-text
`eq:ptildedef`. The tilted integral is not assumed integrable in advance. -/

/-- Taking logs preserves the source's evidence comparison when the tilted
normalizer is positive. Its positivity must be established for the model. -/

/-- Exact finite uniform expectation over the diffusion time index. This is
the arithmetic mean on `Fin K`, so no sampling or asymptotic premise is used. -/

/-- Supplement `app_eq:diffusion_likelihood` and
`app:one_sample_simplified_diffusion`: without inverse-inclusion scaling,
a uniformly selected summand estimates the average, rather than the sum. -/

/-- Corrected unbiased single-time estimator of a *summed* diffusion
objective: multiply the sampled summand by the number of time indices. -/

end LatentDiffusion.SourceResults

`cauchy_minimizing_sequence` corrects Supplement `lem:cauchy`: a Cauchy
sequence must also be a minimizing sequence. A complete ambient metric space
and lower semicontinuity then give an actual minimizer.
-/

/-- Corrected Supplement `lem:cauchy`: completeness and lower semicontinuity
identify the limit of a Cauchy *minimizing* sequence as a minimizer.
No unrelated Cauchy sequence supplies this conclusion. -/

/-- The scalar derivative used in Supplement `app:lemma_1st_var` includes
the additive constant one. It disappears only on zero-total-mass directions. -/

/-- Constants represent the same first variation on probability tangent
directions. This proves the precise reason the source may omit `+1`. -/

/-- The source's normalized product metric cancels the `1/M` from the
distributional first variation with the inverse metric's `M`.
The positivity of the data count is essential. -/

/-- The first-order scalar consequence of the source's geodesic-convexity
inequality. This step is proved by taking the right derivative; the existence
and calculus of an actual Wasserstein geodesic is not a premise hidden here. -/

/-- The source's Talagrand-type quadratic growth follows directly from strong
geodesic convexity at a minimizer. This proof needs no entropy dissipation.
The application must still establish the displayed convexity inequality for
its actual displacement interpolation and actual metric distance. -/

/-- The actual tilted density in main-text `eq:ptildedef`. -/

/-- The log-density free energy used by the paper, relative to a base measure. -/

/-- Pointwise tilt identity, including zeros of the trial density. -/

/-- Main-text free-energy decomposition after `eq:free-energy`, proved for
the actual base-density integral. Both integrable summands are explicit. -/

/-- Nonnegative KL regularization raises the density free energy. The KL
interpretation of `R` is independent of this integral inequality. -/

/-- Integrability and evidence order follow from a nonnegative integrable
base density and a measurable nonnegative penalty, as used after main-text
`eq:ptildedef`. The tilted integral is not assumed integrable in advance. -/

/-- Taking logs preserves the source's evidence comparison when the tilted
normalizer is positive. Its positivity must be established for the model. -/

/-- Exact finite uniform expectation over the diffusion time index. This is
the arithmetic mean on `Fin K`, so no sampling or asymptotic premise is used. -/

/-- Supplement `app_eq:diffusion_likelihood` and
`app:one_sample_simplified_diffusion`: without inverse-inclusion scaling,
a uniformly selected summand estimates the average, rather than the sum. -/

/-- Corrected unbiased single-time estimator of a *summed* diffusion
objective: multiply the sampled summand by the number of time indices. -/

Mathematical statement
The momentum tracks the positive gradient of the descent loss, but the particle update adds it. With that momentum convention, descent requires −hzGM-h_zGM−hz​GM. The loop's particle index is B×[N]\mathcal B\times[N]B×[N], not B×[M]\mathcal B\times[M]B×[M]. The equation scales noise variance by 1/M1/M1/M, and the implementation paragraph adds a further noise-amplitude factor 1/B1/B1/B; these change the sampler. The pseudocode also overwrites its drifted temporary value when adding noise, so the intended update should add drift and noise to the same new state. For a state-dependent preconditioner a target-preserving Langevin diffusion generally needs the appropriate divergence drift; momentum requires an enlarged-state invariant-law analysis. None of these changes is covered by the source's full-batch theorem.

Part II — New theory

The paper already gives a full-batch error rate with implicit constants. These additions make the force geometry, particle variance, discretization and oracle contributions explicit. Their hypotheses are listed first.

What changes for inference?

The final bound separates initialization, particle count, step size and oracle noise, so each source of parameter error can be budgeted.

What changes for minibatches?

Exact variance and scalar temperature calculations distinguish sampling error from a change of target caused by the printed noise scaling.

What changes for model bias?

A one-sided evidence gap turns approximate tilted optimization into an explicit distance from the original model’s optimizer.

New Assumptions — N1–N7

N1 is the force interface, derived from A3–A4 for the scaled cloud. N2 is the step restriction. N3–N4 describe alternative reference formulations; N5–N7 supply the probabilistic inputs for the main bound. Each theorem below names the subset it uses; these premises are not asserted to follow from A1–A4.

New theory

N1 — Monotone, Lipschitz force

Mathematical statement

Let HHH be a real inner-product space. The positive force FFF, equal to minus the drift, satisfies for every x,y∈Hx,y\in Hx,y∈H

λ∥x−y∥2≤⟨F(x)−F(y),x−y⟩,∥F(x)−F(y)∥≤L∥x−y∥,L≥0.\lambda\|x-y\|^2\le\langle F(x)-F(y),x-y\rangle,\qquad \|F(x)-F(y)\|\le L\|x-y\|,\quad L\ge0.λ∥x−y∥2≤⟨F(x)−F(y),x−y⟩,∥F(x)−F(y)∥≤L∥x−y∥,L≥0.

This is an explicit assumption on the complete force of the parameter and particle system in the chosen norm. Applying a per-datapoint hypothesis to that complete system requires its own lifting argument.

import UnadjustedLangevin.GradientStep

/-!
# Quantitative stability and discretization error for latent Euler algorithms

These results concern actual Euler updates on a real inner product space.  In the
paper's interacting algorithm that space can be the latent parameter / particle
cloud with its particle-normalized inner product.  Neither contraction nor an
error recurrence is included among the hypotheses.

The reference-path consistency hypothesis below is a *local defect bound*.  An
SDE application must establish it from the drift and Brownian regularity; this
file does not claim that such a bound follows from monotonicity alone.
-/

open scoped NNReal

namespace LatentDiffusion

variable {H : Type*} [NormedAddCommGroup H] [InnerProductSpace ℝ H]

/-- Added regularity assumption on the positive force, i.e. minus the SDE drift.
The constant `L` is nonnegative by its type. -/

/-- A step restriction stated without division, including degenerate spaces. -/

/-- The Euler update, with the entire additive noise increment supplied as `ξ`.
For IPLD it is `sqrt (2h)` times the appropriately scaled Gaussian cloud. -/

/-- The actual numerical trajectory, rather than an assumed error recurrence. -/

/-- Shared additive noise cancels, and strong monotonicity yields the sharp
quadratic one-step coefficient. -/

/-- A simpler squared contraction with a transparent step restriction. -/

/-- Norm contraction sufficient for robust coupling and numerical consistency. -/

/-- The familiar minimum step restriction implies the division-free one. -/

/-- A single update separates force approximation error from the reference's
local discretization defect. No stochastic independence is required. -/

/-- Finite-horizon robust numerical bound, including the exact geometric factor.
`G` is the implemented force; `F` is the reference force. The reference can be an
exact SDE skeleton once the stated local defect estimate has been established. -/

/-- Uniform numerical and model bias: `2 B / m + (2 D / m) sqrt h`.
The dimension and number of particles do not enter this algebraic estimate. -/

end LatentDiffusion

namespace LatentDiffusion

variable {H : Type*} [NormedAddCommGroup H] [InnerProductSpace ℝ H]

/-- Squared coupling error averaged over a finite probability space. -/

/-- Explicit finite probability weights. Normalization gives the expression its
usual expectation interpretation; the algebraic estimates only need positivity. -/

/-- Euler with a shared additive increment and an additional stochastic force
innovation `ζ`, multiplied by the step size. -/

/-- The zero cross moment needed from a centered innovation is stated on the
current Euler displacement. Conditional mean zero given the current states and
shared increment is a sufficient probabilistic condition for this assumption. -/

/-- Pythagorean identity after averaging: only the explicit cross moment is used. -/

/-- Centered stochastic force error has a mean-square floor of order `h`, rather
than the order-one floor for an arbitrary bounded force error. The result is for
actual coupled Euler recursions on any finite probability space. -/

end LatentDiffusion

namespace LatentDiffusion

open MeasureTheory

variable {H : Type*} [NormedAddCommGroup H] [InnerProductSpace ℝ H] [CompleteSpace H]

/-- Primitive assumptions on exact integral reference segments. In an `L²`
realization `G` bounds the drift root mean square and `N sqrt t` bounds the
Brownian-increment root mean square. These are moment assumptions, not a local
numerical error or contraction assumption. `W` is the additive noise path. -/

/-- The local consistency bound is derived from the exact integral equation,
the drift moment bound, and the square-root noise increment bound. -/

/-- Nonasymptotic Euler error derived from primitive integral-path moment bounds,
with separate numerical bias `O(h G + N sqrt h)` and force-model bias `O(B)`.
The ambient space can be an `L²` Hilbert space, in which case this is an RMS
coupling estimate. An SDE existence theorem and verification of its stated
moment and lifted-force assumptions are separate obligations. -/

end LatentDiffusion

namespace LatentDiffusion

variable {H : Type*} [NormedAddCommGroup H] [InnerProductSpace ℝ H]

/-- Centered local force innovations in a Hilbert space. On `L²(Ω,P;E)`, the
orthogonality field is exactly a zero expected cross term, and the variance
field is a second-moment bound on the stochastic force innovation. -/

import UnadjustedLangevin.GradientStep
import UnadjustedLangevin.Recurrence
import UnadjustedLangevin.LocalError
import Mathlib.Analysis.SpecialFunctions.Exp
import Mathlib.MeasureTheory.Function.L2Space

/-!
# Quantitative stability and discretization error for latent Euler algorithms

These results concern actual Euler updates on a real inner product space.  In the
paper's interacting algorithm that space can be the latent parameter / particle
cloud with its particle-normalized inner product.  Neither contraction nor an
error recurrence is included among the hypotheses.

The reference-path consistency hypothesis below is a *local defect bound*.  An
SDE application must establish it from the drift and Brownian regularity; this
file does not claim that such a bound follows from monotonicity alone.
-/

open scoped NNReal

namespace LatentDiffusion

variable {H : Type*} [NormedAddCommGroup H] [InnerProductSpace ℝ H]

/-- Added regularity assumption on the positive force, i.e. minus the SDE drift.
The constant `L` is nonnegative by its type. -/

/-- A step restriction stated without division, including degenerate spaces. -/

/-- The Euler update, with the entire additive noise increment supplied as `ξ`.
For IPLD it is `sqrt (2h)` times the appropriately scaled Gaussian cloud. -/

/-- The actual numerical trajectory, rather than an assumed error recurrence. -/

/-- Shared additive noise cancels, and strong monotonicity yields the sharp
quadratic one-step coefficient. -/

/-- A simpler squared contraction with a transparent step restriction. -/

/-- Norm contraction sufficient for robust coupling and numerical consistency. -/

/-- The familiar minimum step restriction implies the division-free one. -/

/-- A single update separates force approximation error from the reference's
local discretization defect. No stochastic independence is required. -/

/-- Finite-horizon robust numerical bound, including the exact geometric factor.
`G` is the implemented force; `F` is the reference force. The reference can be an
exact SDE skeleton once the stated local defect estimate has been established. -/

/-- Uniform numerical and model bias: `2 B / m + (2 D / m) sqrt h`.
The dimension and number of particles do not enter this algebraic estimate. -/

end LatentDiffusion

namespace LatentDiffusion

variable {H : Type*} [NormedAddCommGroup H] [InnerProductSpace ℝ H]

/-- Squared coupling error averaged over a finite probability space. -/

/-- Explicit finite probability weights. Normalization gives the expression its
usual expectation interpretation; the algebraic estimates only need positivity. -/

/-- Euler with a shared additive increment and an additional stochastic force
innovation `ζ`, multiplied by the step size. -/

/-- The zero cross moment needed from a centered innovation is stated on the
current Euler displacement. Conditional mean zero given the current states and
shared increment is a sufficient probabilistic condition for this assumption. -/

/-- Pythagorean identity after averaging: only the explicit cross moment is used. -/

/-- Centered stochastic force error has a mean-square floor of order `h`, rather
than the order-one floor for an arbitrary bounded force error. The result is for
actual coupled Euler recursions on any finite probability space. -/

end LatentDiffusion

namespace LatentDiffusion

open MeasureTheory

variable {H : Type*} [NormedAddCommGroup H] [InnerProductSpace ℝ H] [CompleteSpace H]

/-- Primitive assumptions on exact integral reference segments. In an `L²`
realization `G` bounds the drift root mean square and `N sqrt t` bounds the
Brownian-increment root mean square. These are moment assumptions, not a local
numerical error or contraction assumption. `W` is the additive noise path. -/

/-- The local consistency bound is derived from the exact integral equation,
the drift moment bound, and the square-root noise increment bound. -/

/-- Nonasymptotic Euler error derived from primitive integral-path moment bounds,
with separate numerical bias `O(h G + N sqrt h)` and force-model bias `O(B)`.
The ambient space can be an `L²` Hilbert space, in which case this is an RMS
coupling estimate. An SDE existence theorem and verification of its stated
moment and lifted-force assumptions are separate obligations. -/

end LatentDiffusion

namespace LatentDiffusion

variable {H : Type*} [NormedAddCommGroup H] [InnerProductSpace ℝ H]

/-- Centered local force innovations in a Hilbert space. On `L²(Ω,P;E)`, the
orthogonality field is exactly a zero expected cross term, and the variance
field is a second-moment bound on the stochastic force innovation. -/

/-- Uniform second-moment stability for centered stochastic force errors in an
arbitrary real Hilbert space, including genuine `L²` probability spaces. -/

section ArbitraryProbability

open MeasureTheory

variable {Ω E : Type*} [MeasurableSpace Ω]
  [NormedAddCommGroup E] [InnerProductSpace ℝ E]
  (P : Measure Ω) [IsProbabilityMeasure P]

/-- Actual expectation interpretation of the Hilbert squared norm. `Lp` ensures
square integrability of every variable; no totalized nonintegrable expectation
is used as an error metric. -/

/-- Nonasymptotic mean-square stochastic-oracle bound on an arbitrary probability
space, permitting Gaussian innovations. `F` is the explicitly supplied force
on actual `L²` random variables and its monotonicity/Lipschitz assumptions must
hold in `L²`; pointwise cloud assumptions can be lifted separately. -/

end ArbitraryProbability

end LatentDiffusion

New theory

N6 — Frozen reference and empirical-force residual

Mathematical statement

In the genuine space L2(Ω;scaled cloud)L^2(\Omega;\text{scaled cloud})L2(Ω;scaled cloud), a reference force RRR is LLL-Lipschitz and admits actual segments satisfying N4, with nonnegative drift radius GGG and noise bound WtW\sqrt tWt​. It need not contract in the fixed parameter coordinate.

The actual physical parameter projection CCC has norm at most one and satisfies Cyn=a⋆Cy_n=a_\starCyn​=a⋆​ almost surely for every nnn. The norms in N4 are root mean squares. The construction and stationarity of a frozen posterior process, and its uniform drift/noise moment bounds, must be supplied by the application. The theorem accepts any such fixed reference parameter. An inference guarantee to the paper's tilted maximizer additionally identifies this a⋆a_\stara⋆​ with the optimizer proved in Part I.

Theorem New 1 — Uniform inference error with a stochastic oracle

Mathematical statement

Let K=MN>0K=MN>0K=MN>0, and impose A3–A4 on each actual datum potential and N2, N5–N7 on the reference and innovations. Construct the complete interacting force FKF_KFK​ from those potentials, and use its actual noisy Euler update Xn+1=Xn−hFK(Xn)+ξn+hζnX_{n+1}=X_n-hF_K(X_n)+\xi_n+h\zeta_nXn+1​=Xn​−hFK​(Xn​)+ξn​+hζn​. Write an=CXna_n=CX_nan​=CXn​ for the physical parameter and q=1−λh/2q=1-\lambda h/2q=1−λh/2. For every n≥0n\ge0n≥0,

(E∥an−a⋆∥2)1/2≤qn∥X0−y0∥L2+2λVK+Lλ(hG+43Wh)+hσ2λ.\begin{aligned}\left(\mathbb E\|a_n-a_\star\|^2\right)^{1/2}\le{}&q^n\|X_0-y_0\|_{L^2}+\frac2\lambda\sqrt{\frac VK}\\&+\frac L\lambda\left(hG+\frac43W\sqrt h\right)+\sqrt{\frac{h\sigma^2}{\lambda}}.\end{aligned}(E∥an​−a⋆​∥2)1/2≤​qn∥X0​−y0​∥L2​+λ2​KV​​+λL​(hG+34​Wh​)+λhσ2​​.​

The force regularity is derived from the original per-datum potentials, including the exact pointwise-to-L2L^2L2 lift. The output norm is proved equal to the physical parameter root mean-square error. The four explicit terms quantify initialization, finite-particle averaging, temporal discretization and the centered stochastic oracle. The finite-population identity below calibrates oracle variance from batch dispersion.

The bound is uniform in the number of steps. Its target a⋆a_\stara⋆​ is the fixed reference parameter specified in N6; interpreting it as convergence to the paper's optimizer requires that identification and a corresponding frozen posterior reference. It retains explicit reference existence, moment and innovation premises; it does not claim convergence of the unrestricted Adam/preconditioned implementation.

What this adds to the paper. The paper gives an implicit full-batch error rate. This bound shows how much error comes from initialization, a finite particle cloud, finite time steps and a noisy gradient oracle, under the stated reference assumptions.

The stationary-reference integral equation, its primitive drift/noise moments,
and orthogonal centered sampling residuals are explicit added hypotheses.

file does not assert that arbitrary neural potentials satisfy global convexity,

Theorem New 2 — Two explicit minibatch temperature corrections

Mathematical statement

Random scan: select both an uninflated drift and its 2h\sqrt{2h}2h​ noise with probability ppp, leaving the particle fixed otherwise. Its scalar second-moment fixed point is

vscan=1a(1−ah/2).v_{\mathrm{scan}}=\frac1{a(1-ah/2)}.vscan​=a(1−ah/2)1​.

Full noise: retain the inverse-inclusion drift and replace the printed noise by 2h W\sqrt{2h}\,W2h​W on every particle. Its second-moment fixed point is

vfull=1a(1−ah/(2p)).v_{\mathrm{full}}=\frac1{a(1-ah/(2p))}.vfull​=a(1−ah/(2p))1​.

The denominators must be nonzero in the algebraic identities. For meaningful positive stable scalar moments take a>0a>0a>0 and respectively 0<ah<20<ah<20<ah<2 or 0<ah<2p0<ah<2p0<ah<2p. These exact quadratic calculations expose the remaining Euler bias and the 1/p1/p1/p cost of random drift. They do not assert invariant-law existence for the adaptive nonlinear algorithm.

What this adds to the paper. These two scalar repairs restore the intended small-step temperature. They show that changing the batch size can change the target unless drift and noise are scaled consistently.

/-!
# Exact mini-batch noise and temperature audit

For one fixed datum, a uniform batch of size B among M data has inclusion
probability p = B/M. Algorithm 1 uses an inverse-inclusion drift h/p when the
datum is selected, but adds Gaussian noise of variance 2hp to every particle.
The calculations below integrate the actual standard Gaussian; no diffusion
limit or invariant-law assumption is used. In particular, the source's claimed
variance matching fails even for the one-dimensional quadratic potential.

The scalar moment chains are defined recursions, derived from the exact
one-step conditional Gaussian moment. They do not assert existence or
convergence of a nonlinear adaptive Adam sampler.
-/

open MeasureTheory ProbabilityTheory
open scoped NNReal

namespace LatentDiffusion.BatchAudit

/-- Expectation over a Bernoulli selection of marginal probability `p`. -/

/-- The exact inverse-inclusion drift used by the paper's mini-batch update. -/

/-- Inverse-inclusion scaling gives the full drift in expectation. -/

/-- Actual Gaussian conditional second moment, with specified noise variance. -/

/-- The Gaussian integration is proved from its first two moments. -/

/-- The paper noises every particle with variance `2hp`, even if unselected. -/

/-- Exact moment of Algorithm 1 for the quadratic potential `a x²/2`. -/

/-- The exact second-moment contraction coefficient of the paper update. -/

/-- The stability interval is explicit: the scalar moment coefficient is in `[0,1)`. -/

/-- Actual iterated Gaussian integral with a centered Gaussian initial law. -/

/-- The source target loses second moment for every sufficiently small positive step
whenever the batch is a strict subset of the data. -/

/-- A scalar affine moment chain, independent of any assumed final bound. -/

/-- Every time step has an exact, explicit transient about any fixed point. -/

/-- Stationary second moment of the source mini-batch update. -/

/-- The source's stationary moment includes the mini-batch temperature `p`. -/

/-- Exact all-iteration second-moment formula for the source scalar scheme. -/

/-- Starting at target variance one, a half-batch changes it to `7/8` in one step.
Thus the target is not invariant for the source algorithm. -/

/-- A direct target-law counterexample: two Gaussian integrals and the Bernoulli
average give `7/8`, so the intended standard Gaussian cannot be invariant. -/

/-- Constant-temperature Euler–Maruyama moment update. -/

/-- Exact stationary variance of scalar Euler–Maruyama at temperature `τ`. -/

/-- A corrected random-scan update selects BOTH uninflated drift and noise. -/

/-- Random scan preserves the full-batch temperature: both changes have rate `p`. -/

/-- The corrected random-scan stationary second moment has no temperature `p`. -/

/-- Alternative correction: retain inverse-inclusion drift and full noise. -/

/-- Full noise restores temperature one, while random drift keeps a `1/p` cost. -/

/-- The stationary variance for inverse-inclusion drift and corrected full noise. -/

end LatentDiffusion.BatchAudit

New theory

Theorem New 3 — Quantitative robustness to diffusion tilting

Mathematical statement

Let the true evidence ℓ\ellℓ be λ\lambdaλ-strongly concave, λ>0\lambda>0λ>0, with global maximizer a⋆a_\stara⋆​. Assume a uniform one-sided tilting gap and an approximate tilted optimizer:

0≤ℓ(a)−ℓ~(a)≤δ,ℓ~(a)≤ℓ~(a^)+εfor every a,δ,ε≥0.0\le\ell(a)-\tilde\ell(a)\le\delta,\qquad\tilde\ell(a)\le\tilde\ell(\hat a)+\varepsilon\quad\text{for every }a,\qquad\delta,\varepsilon\ge0.0≤ℓ(a)−ℓ~(a)≤δ,ℓ~(a)≤ℓ~(a^)+εfor every a,δ,ε≥0.

Then both the true-objective and true-parameter errors are controlled:

ℓ(a⋆)−ℓ(a^)≤δ+ε,∥a^−a⋆∥≤2(δ+ε)λ.\ell(a_\star)-\ell(\hat a)\le\delta+\varepsilon,\qquad\|\hat a-a_\star\|\le\sqrt{\frac{2(\delta+\varepsilon)}\lambda}.ℓ(a⋆​)−ℓ(a^)≤δ+ε,∥a^−a⋆​∥≤λ2(δ+ε)​​.

This quantifies the source's expressiveness discussion with an explicit model-bias assumption; it does not infer a uniform evidence gap from a pointwise training penalty.

What this adds to the paper. The paper optimizes a tilted model. This result quantifies how close its approximate optimizer is to the original model's optimizer when a uniform evidence-gap bound is available.

New theory

Theorem New 4 — Sharp Euler contraction

Mathematical statement

Under N1 and h≥0h\ge0h≥0, the same increment cancels in two Euler updates:

∥EF(x,ξ)−EF(y,ξ)∥2≤(1−2λh+L2h2)∥x−y∥2.\|E_F(x,\xi)-E_F(y,\xi)\|^2\le(1-2\lambda h+L^2h^2)\|x-y\|^2.∥EF​(x,ξ)−EF​(y,ξ)∥2≤(1−2λh+L2h2)∥x−y∥2.

Under N2 this gives, with q=1−λh/2∈[0,1)q=1-\lambda h/2\in[0,1)q=1−λh/2∈[0,1),

∥EF(x,ξ)−EF(y,ξ)∥≤q∥x−y∥.\|E_F(x,\xi)-E_F(y,\xi)\|\le q\|x-y\|.∥EF​(x,ξ)−EF​(y,ξ)∥≤q∥x−y∥.

The result holds for arbitrary common increments and the actual update map.

What this adds to the paper. Two updates driven by the same noise move closer together. This is the stability mechanism that prevents small numerical errors from accumulating indefinitely.

/-!
# Quantitative stability and discretization error for latent Euler algorithms

These results concern actual Euler updates on a real inner product space.  In the
paper's interacting algorithm that space can be the latent parameter / particle
cloud with its particle-normalized inner product.  Neither contraction nor an
error recurrence is included among the hypotheses.

The reference-path consistency hypothesis below is a *local defect bound*.  An
SDE application must establish it from the drift and Brownian regularity; this
file does not claim that such a bound follows from monotonicity alone.
-/

open scoped NNReal

namespace LatentDiffusion

variable {H : Type*} [NormedAddCommGroup H] [InnerProductSpace ℝ H]

/-- Added regularity assumption on the positive force, i.e. minus the SDE drift.
The constant `L` is nonnegative by its type. -/

/-- A step restriction stated without division, including degenerate spaces. -/

/-- The Euler update, with the entire additive noise increment supplied as `ξ`.

New theory

Theorem New 5 — Count-independent full-batch contraction

Mathematical statement

Let K=MN>0K=MN>0K=MN>0 count all datum–particle pairs. Give every coordinate its own datum potential UiU_iUi​, each satisfying A3–A4 with the same λ,L\lambda,Lλ,L. Use scaled state s=(a,z1/K,…,zK/K)s=(a,z_1/\sqrt K,\ldots,z_K/\sqrt K)s=(a,z1​/K​,…,zK​/K​), and put

FK(s)=1K∇s∑i=1KUi(a,K si),∥s−sˉ∥2=∥a−aˉ∥2+1K∑i∥zi−zˉi∥2.F_K(s)=\frac1K\nabla_s\sum_{i=1}^K U_i(a,\sqrt K\,s_i),\qquad\|s-\bar s\|^2=\|a-\bar a\|^2+\frac1K\sum_i\|z_i-\bar z_i\|^2.FK​(s)=K1​∇s​i=1∑K​Ui​(a,K​si​),∥s−sˉ∥2=∥a−aˉ∥2+K1​i∑​∥zi​−zˉi​∥2.

The full force FKF_KFK​ is λ\lambdaλ-strongly monotone and LLL-Lipschitz with exactly the original pair constants. Thus, under N2, the actual Euler map contracts synchronously:

∥EFK(s,ξ)−EFK(sˉ,ξ)∥≤(1−λh/2)∥s−sˉ∥.\|E_{F_K}(s,\xi)-E_{F_K}(\bar s,\xi)\|\le(1-\lambda h/2)\|s-\bar s\|.∥EFK​​(s,ξ)−EFK​​(sˉ,ξ)∥≤(1−λh/2)∥s−sˉ∥.

The step restriction and contraction constant are independent of both data and particle counts. The coordinate-gradient identities are checked from the full lifted potential.

What this adds to the paper. Adding more particles does not weaken contraction when the cloud norm averages their squared errors. The proof explains which geometry preserves the paper's original constants.

/-- Extract the scaled latent vector of particle `i`. -/

New theory

Theorem New 6 — Uniform discretization and model-bias budget

Mathematical statement

Under N1–N3, for every integer n≥0n\ge0n≥0,

∥Xn−yn∥≤qn∥X0−y0∥+(hB+Dhh)1−qn1−q≤qn∥X0−y0∥+2λ(B+Dh).\begin{aligned}\|X_n-y_n\|&\le q^n\|X_0-y_0\|+(hB+Dh\sqrt h)\frac{1-q^n}{1-q}\\&\le q^n\|X_0-y_0\|+\frac2\lambda(B+D\sqrt h).\end{aligned}∥Xn​−yn​∥​≤qn∥X0​−y0​∥+(hB+Dhh​)1−q1−qn​≤qn∥X0​−y0​∥+λ2​(B+Dh​).​

The bound separates the initial error, implemented-force bias and temporal consistency. Its constants are explicit and the error floor is uniform in the number of steps. Particle-count or dimension dependence can enter through λ,L,B,D\lambda,L,B,Dλ,L,B,D.

What this adds to the paper. A persistent force error produces a fixed error floor. This separates errors in the implemented gradient from errors caused by discretizing time.

Theorem New 8 — Stochastic-oracle mean-square error floor

Mathematical statement

Under N1, N2 and N5,

∥Xn−Yn∥2≤(1−λh)n∥X0−Y0∥2+hσ2λ.\|X_n-Y_n\|^2\le(1-\lambda h)^n\|X_0-Y_0\|^2+\frac{h\sigma^2}{\lambda}.∥Xn​−Yn​∥2≤(1−λh)n∥X0​−Y0​∥2+λhσ2​.

For the actual Hilbert space L2(Ω,P;E)L^2(\Omega,P;E)L2(Ω,P;E) of square-integrable random variables on an arbitrary probability space, this is the genuine expectation bound

E∥Xn−Yn∥2≤(1−λh)nE∥X0−Y0∥2+hσ2λ.\mathbb E\|X_n-Y_n\|^2\le(1-\lambda h)^n\mathbb E\|X_0-Y_0\|^2+\frac{h\sigma^2}{\lambda}.E∥Xn​−Yn​∥2≤(1−λh)nE∥X0​−Y0​∥2+λhσ2​.

The force regularity in this version is an explicit L2L^2L2 premise. The theorem accepts Gaussian innovations and does not replace nonintegrable expectations by totalized real values.

What this adds to the paper. Centered gradient noise accumulates in mean square. The explicit square-root-in-step-size error floor shows how reducing the step size controls this additional source of error.

with separate numerical bias `O(h G + N sqrt h)` and force-model bias `O(B)`.
The ambient space can be an `L²` Hilbert space, in which case this is an RMS
coupling estimate. An SDE existence theorem and verification of its stated
moment and lifted-force assumptions are separate obligations. -/

end LatentDiffusion

namespace LatentDiffusion

variable {H : Type*} [NormedAddCommGroup H] [InnerProductSpace ℝ H]

/-- Centered local force innovations in a Hilbert space. On `L²(Ω,P;E)`, the
orthogonality field is exactly a zero expected cross term, and the variance
field is a second-moment bound on the stochastic force innovation. -/

/-- Uniform second-moment stability for centered stochastic force errors in an
arbitrary real Hilbert space, including genuine `L²` probability spaces. -/

section ArbitraryProbability

open MeasureTheory

variable {Ω E : Type*} [MeasurableSpace Ω]
  [NormedAddCommGroup E] [InnerProductSpace ℝ E]
  (P : Measure Ω) [IsProbabilityMeasure P]

/-- Actual expectation interpretation of the Hilbert squared norm. `Lp` ensures
square integrability of every variable; no totalized nonintegrable expectation
is used as an error metric. -/

/-- Nonasymptotic mean-square stochastic-oracle bound on an arbitrary probability
space, permitting Gaussian innovations. `F` is the explicitly supplied force
on actual `L²` random variables and its monotonicity/Lipschitz assumptions must
hold in `L²`; pointwise cloud assumptions can be lifted separately. -/

405theorem l2_innovation_mean_square_bound406    (F : Lp E 2 P → Lp E 2 P) (m h σ : ℝ) (L : ℝ≥0)407    (hF : ForceRegularity F m L) (hs : StableStep m L h)408    (ξ ζ : ℕ → Lp E 2 P) (x₀ y₀ : Lp E 2 P)409    (hc : HilbertInnovationControl F h σ ξ ζ x₀ y₀) (n : ℕ) :410    (∫ ω, ‖(eulerTrajectory F h (fun k ↦ ξ k + h • ζ k) x₀ n -411      eulerTrajectory F h ξ y₀ n) ω‖ ^ 2 ∂P) ≤412        (1 - m * h) ^ n * (∫ ω, ‖(x₀ - y₀) ω‖ ^ 2 ∂P) + h * σ ^ 2 / m
New theory

Theorem New 9 — Genuine probability-space lift of the pointwise force

Mathematical statement

On any probability space, a pointwise force F:E→EF:E\to EF:E→E satisfying N1 induces a genuine operator F:L2(Ω;E)→L2(Ω;E)\mathscr F:L^2(\Omega;E)\to L^2(\Omega;E)F:L2(Ω;E)→L2(Ω;E) with

(FX)(ω)=F(X(ω))almost surely.(\mathscr F X)(\omega)=F(X(\omega))\quad\text{almost surely}.(FX)(ω)=F(X(ω))almost surely.

The lifted force inherits the same monotonicity and Lipschitz constants. Its Euler iterates agree almost surely with the pointwise recursion. Therefore the stochastic-oracle expectation bound holds from regularity of the original pointwise force, together with N2 and the explicit innovation condition N5:

E∥Xn−Yn∥2≤(1−λh)nE∥X0−Y0∥2+hσ2λ.\mathbb E\|X_n-Y_n\|^2\le(1-\lambda h)^n\mathbb E\|X_0-Y_0\|^2+\frac{h\sigma^2}{\lambda}.E∥Xn​−Yn​∥2≤(1−λh)nE∥X0​−Y0​∥2+λhσ2​.

No separate lifted-force regularity assumption or condition F(0)=0F(0)=0F(0)=0 is needed.

What this adds to the paper. This connects regularity of the actual force on particle states to expected-error bounds for random states. It justifies applying the numerical argument on a real probability space.

liftedForce_coe · complete proof

Exact shared Lean context
import LatentDiffusion.Numerics
import Mathlib.MeasureTheory.Function.LpSpace.Basic

/-!
# From pointwise cloud forces to actual square-integrable random variables

The force at the origin need not vanish. We center the force before applying
mathlib's Lipschitz composition operator on `L²`, then add its constant value
back. The resulting operator is proved to agree almost everywhere with the
original pointwise force. Its strong monotonicity and Lipschitz constants are
derived by integration; they are not added assumptions on a random-force map.
-/

noncomputable section
open MeasureTheory
open scoped NNReal

namespace LatentDiffusion

variable {Ω E : Type*} [MeasurableSpace Ω]
  [NormedAddCommGroup E] [InnerProductSpace ℝ E] [CompleteSpace E]
  (P : Measure Ω) [IsProbabilityMeasure P]

/-- A genuine constant square-integrable random variable. -/


/-- The centered pointwise force always takes zero to zero. -/


/-- The actual force acting on `L²` random variables; no zero-force condition. -/

/-- This operator really evaluates the given pointwise force almost everywhere. -/

/-- Pointwise joint monotonicity and global Lipschitz continuity lift with exactly
the same constants, on every probability space. -/

/-- An `L²` Euler step is the actual pointwise Euler step almost everywhere. -/

/-- Every iterate represents the pointwise recursion, for arbitrary square-
integrable increments, including actual Gaussian innovations. -/

/-- Mean-square numerical robustness is now a consequence of assumptions on the
original pointwise force, with no independently assumed `L²` force regularity. -/

end LatentDiffusion

New theory

Theorem New 10 — Heterogeneous particle-average variance

Mathematical statement

Let K>0K>0K>0, and let g1,…,gKg_1,\ldots,g_Kg1​,…,gK​ be vectors in a real Hilbert space, such as centered random force errors in L2L^2L2. If ⟨gi,gj⟩=0\langle g_i,g_j\rangle=0⟨gi​,gj​⟩=0 for i≠ji\ne ji=j, then

∥1K∑igi∥2=1K2∑i∥gi∥2≤VKwhen ∥gi∥2≤V.\left\|\frac1K\sum_i g_i\right\|^2=\frac1{K^2}\sum_i\|g_i\|^2\le\frac VK\quad\text{when }\|g_i\|^2\le V.​K1​i∑​gi​​2=K21​i∑​∥gi​∥2≤KV​when ∥gi​∥2≤V.

Hence a residual represented by this average has B≤V/KB\le\sqrt{V/K}B≤V/K​. The copies may have different laws, as occurs for different data. Orthogonality is the explicit cross-moment premise; independence and centering must be verified when used to establish it.

What this adds to the paper. Different data can have different posterior laws. Zero cross moments still give inverse-square-root particle averaging, so identical distributions across data are unnecessary.

Exact shared Lean context
import LatentDiffusion.Numerics
import Mathlib.Analysis.InnerProductSpace.Basic
import Mathlib.MeasureTheory.Integral.Bochner.SumMeasure

/-!
# Explicit averaging variance for heterogeneous particles and mini-batches

Orthogonality is a primitive centered cross-moment assumption in `L²`; it does
not require identically distributed copies. Thus particles belonging to
different data may have different laws. The mini-batch results below use
primitive first and pair inclusion probabilities, not an assumed oracle-error
bound.
-/

noncomputable section
open MeasureTheory
open scoped BigOperators NNReal

namespace LatentDiffusion.MiniBatchVariance

variable {H : Type*} [NormedAddCommGroup H] [InnerProductSpace ℝ H]

/-- Actual normalized sum, also used for `L²` random variables. -/

/-- Pythagoras for a heterogeneous family with zero cross inner products. -/

/-- Exact second moment of a centered orthogonal particle average. -/

/-- A per-copy variance bound gives `V/K` without identical-distribution assumptions. -/

/-- Root mean-square version used for the empirical parameter-force residual. -/

/-- Expanding the squared norm, retaining every heterogeneous cross term. -/

/-- Centering each heterogeneous vector by the full population average gives
exactly zero total; no assumption on the individual means is needed. -/


/-- Exchangeable inclusion moments separate a diagonal variance and a mean term. -/

section FiniteBatch

variable {Ω : Type*} [Fintype Ω] [MeasurableSpace Ω] [MeasurableSingletonClass Ω]
  (P : Measure Ω) [IsProbabilityMeasure P]

/-- The indicator of selecting datum `i` in the actual sampled batch. -/

/-- Primitive uniform fixed-size sampling laws. These are first and pair
inclusion probabilities of an actual finite probability distribution, not a
variance bound or a recurrence assumption. -/

/-- The actual mini-batch average of the supplied centered per-datum vectors. -/

/-- The sum of selection indicators is the actual batch cardinality. -/

/-- Fixed batch cardinality makes centering commute with the sampled average. -/

/-- The two primitive inclusion laws determine every indicator-product moment. -/

/-- Exact expectation of the unnormalized sampled sum; finite probability makes
all polynomial integrals genuine finite integrals. -/

/-- Exact finite-population correction for mini-batching without replacement.
The vectors may be heterogeneous; only their total centered sum is zero. -/

/-- The familiar exact variance formula, directly for the raw gradient oracle
minus the full-data gradient, with finite-population correction. -/

/-- Explicit squared oracle-noise scale, computed from batch and data sizes. -/

/-- A population gradient-dispersion bound gives the derived mini-batch oracle
variance used by the stochastic Euler theorem. -/

end FiniteBatch

end LatentDiffusion.MiniBatchVariance

New theory

Theorem New 11 — Exact minibatch finite-population correction

Mathematical statement

Let M>1M>1M>1, b>0b>0b>0. An actual finite probability space carries batches of size bbb, with inclusion probabilities

P(i∈B)=bM,P(i,j∈B)=b(b−1)M(M−1)(i≠j).\mathbb P(i\in\mathcal B)=\frac bM,\qquad\mathbb P(i,j\in\mathcal B)=\frac{b(b-1)}{M(M-1)}\quad(i\ne j).P(i∈B)=Mb​,P(i,j∈B)=M(M−1)b(b−1)​(i=j).

For arbitrary heterogeneous per-datum gradients gig_igi​, put gˉ=M−1∑igi\bar g=M^{-1}\sum_i g_igˉ​=M−1∑i​gi​. The actual raw-gradient oracle obeys

E∥1b∑i∈Bgi−gˉ∥2=M−bb(M−1) 1M∑i∥gi−gˉ∥2.\mathbb E\left\|\frac1b\sum_{i\in\mathcal B}g_i-\bar g\right\|^2=\frac{M-b}{b(M-1)}\,\frac1M\sum_i\|g_i-\bar g\|^2.E​b1​i∈B∑​gi​−gˉ​​2=b(M−1)M−b​M1​i∑​∥gi​−gˉ​∥2.

For b≤Mb\le Mb≤M, a population dispersion bound M−1∑i∥gi−gˉ∥2≤VM^{-1}\sum_i\|g_i-\bar g\|^2\le VM−1∑i​∥gi​−gˉ​∥2≤V therefore gives the derived oracle variance σ2≤(M−b)V/[b(M−1)]\sigma^2\le (M-b)V/[b(M-1)]σ2≤(M−b)V/[b(M−1)]. The theorem derives this from the primitive first and pair inclusion laws, including zero sampling variance at full batch. Applying this identity to the whole-cloud stochastic force requires its actual scaled blocks and inverse-inclusion factors: the dispersion VVV may depend on both MMM and NNN, so a count-independent σ2\sigma^2σ2 bound does not follow automatically.

What this adds to the paper. The variance formula accounts for sampling data without replacement. It vanishes at full batch and exposes the batch-size factor needed to calibrate the oracle term.

/-!
# Explicit averaging variance for heterogeneous particles and mini-batches

Orthogonality is a primitive centered cross-moment assumption in `L²`; it does
not require identically distributed copies. Thus particles belonging to
different data may have different laws. The mini-batch results below use
primitive first and pair inclusion probabilities, not an assumed oracle-error
bound.
-/

noncomputable section
open MeasureTheory
open scoped BigOperators NNReal

namespace LatentDiffusion.MiniBatchVariance

variable {H : Type*} [NormedAddCommGroup H] [InnerProductSpace ℝ H]

/-- Pythagoras for a heterogeneous family with zero cross inner products. -/

/-- Exact second moment of a centered orthogonal particle average. -/

/-- A per-copy variance bound gives `V/K` without identical-distribution assumptions. -/

/-- Root mean-square version used for the empirical parameter-force residual. -/

/-- Expanding the squared norm, retaining every heterogeneous cross term. -/

/-- Centering each heterogeneous vector by the full population average gives
exactly zero total; no assumption on the individual means is needed. -/


/-- Exchangeable inclusion moments separate a diagonal variance and a mean term. -/

section FiniteBatch

  (P : Measure Ω) [IsProbabilityMeasure P]

/-- The indicator of selecting datum `i` in the actual sampled batch. -/

/-- Primitive uniform fixed-size sampling laws. These are first and pair
inclusion probabilities of an actual finite probability distribution, not a
variance bound or a recurrence assumption. -/

/-- The actual mini-batch average of the supplied centered per-datum vectors. -/

/-- The sum of selection indicators is the actual batch cardinality. -/

/-- Fixed batch cardinality makes centering commute with the sampled average. -/

/-- The two primitive inclusion laws determine every indicator-product moment. -/

/-- Exact expectation of the unnormalized sampled sum; finite probability makes
all polynomial integrals genuine finite integrals. -/

/-- Exact finite-population correction for mini-batching without replacement.
The vectors may be heterogeneous; only their total centered sum is zero. -/

/-- The familiar exact variance formula, directly for the raw gradient oracle
minus the full-data gradient, with finite-population correction. -/

/-- Explicit squared oracle-noise scale, computed from batch and data sizes. -/

/-- A population gradient-dispersion bound gives the derived mini-batch oracle
variance used by the stochastic Euler theorem. -/

end FiniteBatch

end LatentDiffusion.MiniBatchVariance

Let ε>0\varepsilon>0ε>0 and R0=∥X0−y0∥L2R_0=\|X_0-y_0\|_{L^2}R0​=∥X0​−y0​∥L2​. Under the preceding main bound, the following explicit conditions suffice for parameter RMS error at most ε\varepsilonε:

λhn2≥log⁡max⁡ ⁣{1,5R0ε},100V≤λ2ε2K,5LhG≤λε,400L2W2h≤9λ2ε2,25hσ2≤λε2.\begin{gathered}\frac{\lambda h n}{2}\ge\log\max\!\left\{1,\frac{5R_0}{\varepsilon}\right\},\qquad100V\le\lambda^2\varepsilon^2K,\\5LhG\le\lambda\varepsilon,\qquad400L^2W^2h\le9\lambda^2\varepsilon^2,\qquad25h\sigma^2\le\lambda\varepsilon^2.\end{gathered}2λhn​≥logmax{1,ε5R0​​},100V≤λ2ε2K,5LhG≤λε,400L2W2h≤9λ2ε2,25hσ2≤λε2.​

Each of the five initialization, particle, drift, noise-modulus and oracle terms receives ε/5\varepsilon/5ε/5. The conditions are division-free, including zero drift, noise or variance constants. The burn-in formula also covers zero initial error. The probabilistic/reference premises remain those of the main theorem.

What this adds to the paper. The implicit rate becomes concrete sufficient inequalities for particle count, step size and burn-in. Each of the five error terms receives one fifth of the requested tolerance.

The mathematical argument

The argument below proves the results in order. The adjacent panels give the exact Lean statements it rests on and explain how the formal proof assembles them.

01Variational characterization of the evidence §

This section proves the variational characterization of the evidence. Let M≥1M\ge1M≥1 be the number of data, let A\mathcal AA be an arbitrary set of parameters and let ZZZ be a measurable space of latent variables. A posterior family consists of a real function ℓ:A→R\ell:\mathcal A\to\mathbb Rℓ:A→R, the log evidence, and, for each parameter a∈Aa\in\mathcal Aa∈A and each datum m∈{1,…,M}m\in\{1,\dots,M\}m∈{1,…,M}, a probability measure πam\pi_a^mπam​ on ZZZ, the posterior of datum mmm. For a collection q=(q1,…,qM)q=(q^1,\dots,q^M)q=(q1,…,qM) of probability measures on ZZZ, the free energy is

F(a,q)=−ℓ(a)+1M∑m=1MKL(qm∥πam),F(a,q)=-\ell(a)+\frac1M\sum_{m=1}^M\mathrm{KL}(q^m\|\pi_a^m),F(a,q)=−ℓ(a)+M1​m=1∑M​KL(qm∥πam​),

where KL\mathrm{KL}KL denotes relative entropy. We prove that F(a,q)≥−ℓ(a)F(a,q)\ge-\ell(a)F(a,q)≥−ℓ(a), with equality exactly when qm=πamq^m=\pi_a^mqm=πam​ for every mmm, and deduce the corrected form of the paper's Proposition 1: a pair (a⋆,q⋆)(a_\star,q_\star)(a⋆​,q⋆​) minimizes FFF among all pairs with finite relative entropies if and only if a⋆a_\stara⋆​ maximizes ℓ\ellℓ and q⋆m=πa⋆mq_\star^m=\pi_{a_\star}^mq⋆m​=πa⋆​m​ for every mmm. No existence of a maximizer is asserted; existence and uniqueness are proved later from strong convexity of the marginal potential.

In the application A\mathcal AA is the space of parameters a=(θ,ϕ)a=(\theta,\phi)a=(θ,ϕ), πam\pi_a^mπam​ is the normalized tilted posterior Zm(a)−1e−Um(a,z) dzZ_m(a)^{-1}e^{-U_m(a,z)}\,dzZm​(a)−1e−Um​(a,z)dz of datum mmm, and ℓ(a)=M−1∑mlog⁡Zm(a)\ell(a)=M^{-1}\sum_m\log Z_m(a)ℓ(a)=M−1∑m​logZm​(a) is the average tilted log evidence. The results hold for every parameter set and every measurable latent space, in particular for tilted models. The last step shows that a zero tilting penalty at a maximizer of the tilted evidence does not identify a maximizer of the original evidence, and gives a sufficient condition that does.

Claim. Let M≥1M\ge1M≥1, a∈Aa\in\mathcal Aa∈A, and let qqq be a collection of MMM probability measures on ZZZ. Then (a,q)(a,q)(a,q) is a global minimizer of FFF if and only if

ℓ(b)≤ℓ(a)  for every b∈Aandqm=πam  for every m.\ell(b)\le\ell(a)\ \text{ for every }b\in\mathcal A\qquad\text{and}\qquad q^m=\pi_a^m\ \text{ for every }m.ℓ(b)≤ℓ(a)  for every b∈Aandqm=πam​  for every m.

Proof. (⇒\Rightarrow⇒) Let (a,q)(a,q)(a,q) be a global minimizer; in particular qqq is admissible at aaa. The posterior collection πa\pi_aπa​ is admissible at aaa, so minimality and the posterior identity of the second step give

F(a,q)≤F(a,πa)=−ℓ(a).F(a,q)\le F(a,\pi_a)=-\ell(a).F(a,q)≤F(a,πa​)=−ℓ(a).

The lower bound of the second step gives F(a,q)≥−ℓ(a)F(a,q)\ge-\ell(a)F(a,q)≥−ℓ(a); hence F(a,q)=−ℓ(a)F(a,q)=-\ell(a)F(a,q)=−ℓ(a), and the previous step yields q=πaq=\pi_aq=πa​. Now let b∈Ab\in\mathcal Ab∈A. Since πb\pi_bπb​ is admissible at bbb, minimality gives

−ℓ(a)=F(a,q)≤F(b,πb)=−ℓ(b),-\ell(a)=F(a,q)\le F(b,\pi_b)=-\ell(b),−ℓ(a)=F(a,q)≤F(b,πb​)=−ℓ(b),

that is, ℓ(b)≤ℓ(a)\ell(b)\le\ell(a)ℓ(b)≤ℓ(a).

(⇐\Leftarrow⇐) Suppose aaa maximizes ℓ\ellℓ and q=πaq=\pi_aq=πa​. Then qqq is admissible at aaa. For every bbb and every rrr admissible at bbb, the posterior identity, the maximality of aaa and the lower bound at bbb give

F(a,πa)=−ℓ(a)≤−ℓ(b)≤F(b,r).F(a,\pi_a)=-\ell(a)\le-\ell(b)\le F(b,r).F(a,πa​)=−ℓ(a)≤−ℓ(b)≤F(b,r).

Thus (a,πa)(a,\pi_a)(a,πa​) is a global minimizer. □\square□

The statement asserts neither that ℓ\ellℓ has a maximizer nor that a maximizer is unique; both questions are settled later for strongly convex potentials. The normalized posterior collection is the unique optimal variational collection at each maximizer.

How the Lean proof follows this argument

global_minimizers_iff states the equivalence for P.IsGlobalMin a q; the right-hand side is the conjunction of ∀ b, P.logEvidence b ≤ P.logEvidence a and q = P.posterior a.

  1. Forward direction: rintro ⟨hq, hmin⟩ splits the hypothesis into admissibility and minimality. he is the identity F(a,q)=−ℓ(a)F(a,q)=-\ell(a)F(a,q)=−ℓ(a), obtained by le_antisymm from hmin a (P.posterior a) (P.posterior_admissible a), rewritten with P.posterior_freeEnergy, and from P.lower_bound a q. The second component is (P.equality_iff hM a q hq).mp he. For the first component, hb applies minimality against (b,πb)(b,\pi_b)(b,πb​), and after rewriting with he and P.posterior_freeEnergy, linarith turns −ℓ(a)≤−ℓ(b)-\ell(a)\le-\ell(b)−ℓ(a)≤−ℓ(b) into ℓ(b)≤ℓ(a)\ell(b)\le\ell(a)ℓ(b)≤ℓ(a).
  2. Reverse direction: rintro ⟨hmax, rfl⟩ substitutes q=πaq=\pi_aq=πa​. Admissibility is P.posterior_admissible a. For an admissible pair (b,r)(b,r)(b,r) the chain of the proof is (neg_le_neg (hmax b)).trans (P.lower_bound b r), after rewriting F(a,πa)F(a,\pi_a)F(a,πa​) by P.posterior_freeEnergy.

02Unique maximizer of the marginal evidence §

For each datum m∈{1,…,M}m\in\{1,\dots,M\}m∈{1,…,M} let Um:Rdθ×Rdz→RU_m:\mathbb R^{d_\theta}\times\mathbb R^{d_z}\to\mathbb RUm​:Rdθ​×Rdz​→R be the joint potential, the negative logarithm of the tilted joint density of the parameter aaa and the latent variable zzz. The pair space carries the Euclidean norm ∥(a,z)∥2=∥a∥2+∥z∥2\|(a,z)\|^2=\|a\|^2+\|z\|^2∥(a,z)∥2=∥a∥2+∥z∥2. Assumption A3 states that each UmU_mUm​ is differentiable and λ\lambdaλ-strongly convex with one constant λ>0\lambda>0λ>0:

Um(sx+(1−s)y)≤sUm(x)+(1−s)Um(y)−λ2s(1−s)∥x−y∥2(x,y∈Rdθ+dz, s∈[0,1]).U_m(sx+(1-s)y)\le sU_m(x)+(1-s)U_m(y)-\frac\lambda2s(1-s)\|x-y\|^2\qquad(x,y\in\mathbb R^{d_\theta+d_z},\ s\in[0,1]).Um​(sx+(1−s)y)≤sUm​(x)+(1−s)Um​(y)−2λ​s(1−s)∥x−y∥2(x,y∈Rdθ​+dz​, s∈[0,1]).

The normalizer and the marginal potential of datum mmm are

Zm(a)=∫Rdze−Um(a,z) dz,Vm(a)=−log⁡Zm(a),V(a)=1M∑m=1MVm(a)=−ℓ(a),Z_m(a)=\int_{\mathbb R^{d_z}}e^{-U_m(a,z)}\,dz,\qquad V_m(a)=-\log Z_m(a),\qquad V(a)=\frac1M\sum_{m=1}^MV_m(a)=-\ell(a),Zm​(a)=∫Rdz​​e−Um​(a,z)dz,Vm​(a)=−logZm​(a),V(a)=M1​m=1∑M​Vm​(a)=−ℓ(a),

so VVV is minus the average log evidence ℓ\ellℓ. This section proves that VVV is λ\lambdaλ-strongly convex, tends to +∞+\infty+∞ at infinity and has exactly one minimizer a⋆a_\stara⋆​; that for every posterior family with log evidence −V-V−V the free energy has exactly one global minimizer (a⋆,πa⋆)(a_\star,\pi_{a_\star})(a⋆​,πa⋆​​); and that VVV grows quadratically away from a⋆a_\stara⋆​. The last step quantifies the effect of the tilting on the optimizer. The unique minimizer is the target of all convergence results of this report.

Claim. Let M≥1M\ge1M≥1, λ>0\lambda>0λ>0, and let every UmU_mUm​ be differentiable and λ\lambdaλ-strongly convex. Then there is exactly one a⋆∈Rdθa_\star\in\mathbb R^{d_\theta}a⋆​∈Rdθ​ with V(a⋆)≤V(a)V(a_\star)\le V(a)V(a⋆​)≤V(a) for all aaa. Equivalently, the average log evidence ℓ=−V\ell=-Vℓ=−V has exactly one maximizer.

Proof. Continuity. Each VmV_mVm​ is continuous (companion report: the normalizer is continuous and positive, and log⁡\loglog is continuous on (0,∞)(0,\infty)(0,∞)); hence VVV, a constant multiple of a finite sum, is continuous.

Existence. Fix a0a_0a0​. By the previous step there is RRR with V(a)>V(a0)V(a)>V(a_0)V(a)>V(a0​) for ∥a∥≥R\|a\|\ge R∥a∥≥R. The closed ball BˉR={∥a∥≤R}\bar B_R=\{\|a\|\le R\}BˉR​={∥a∥≤R} is compact (Heine–Borel) and nonempty, since a0∈BˉRa_0\in\bar B_Ra0​∈BˉR​. A continuous function on a nonempty compact set attains its minimum, say at a⋆∈BˉRa_\star\in\bar B_Ra⋆​∈BˉR​. Then V(a⋆)≤V(a)V(a_\star)\le V(a)V(a⋆​)≤V(a) for a∈BˉRa\in\bar B_Ra∈BˉR​, and for ∥a∥≥R\|a\|\ge R∥a∥≥R we have V(a)>V(a0)≥V(a⋆)V(a)>V(a_0)\ge V(a_\star)V(a)>V(a0​)≥V(a⋆​). Thus a⋆a_\stara⋆​ is a global minimizer.

Uniqueness. Let aaa and bbb both be global minimizers, so V(a)=V(b)=min⁡VV(a)=V(b)=\min VV(a)=V(b)=minV. Strong convexity with α=β=12\alpha=\beta=\frac12α=β=21​ gives

V(a+b2)≤V(a)+V(b)2−λ8∥a−b∥2=min⁡V−λ8∥a−b∥2.V\Bigl(\frac{a+b}2\Bigr)\le\frac{V(a)+V(b)}2-\frac\lambda8\|a-b\|^2=\min V-\frac\lambda8\|a-b\|^2.V(2a+b​)≤2V(a)+V(b)​−8λ​∥a−b∥2=minV−8λ​∥a−b∥2.

If a≠ba\ne ba=b, the right side is strictly smaller than min⁡V\min VminV because λ>0\lambda>0λ>0, which is impossible. Hence a=ba=ba=b. □\square□

How the Lean proof follows this argument

The conclusion ∃! θ, ∀ θ', averageMarginalPotential U θ ≤ averageMarginalPotential U θ' is “there exists a unique global minimizer”.

  1. hc proves continuity from IPLA.marginalPotential_continuous, continuous_finsetSum and multiplication by a constant.
  2. hc.exists_forall_le is Mathlib's Continuous.exists_forall_le: a continuous function that tends to +∞+\infty+∞ along cocompact has a global minimum. Its coercivity input is the previous step. This packages the compactness argument of the proof.
  3. Uniqueness: StrongConvexOn.strictConvexOn turns strong convexity with hrho : 0 < rho into strict convexity, and StrictConvexOn.eq_of_isMinOn states that a strictly convex function has at most one minimizer on a convex set; its proof is the midpoint argument above.

03The density model and its unique optimizer §

This section constructs the tilted latent model from the joint potentials U1,…,UMU_1,\dots,U_MU1​,…,UM​ of assumption A3 and identifies its optimizer. 04De Bruijn identity for the joint flow §

This section proves the de Bruijn identity for the joint parameter–density flow of the paper, under explicit regularity hypotheses (R2, R3). The latent space EEE is a finite-dimensional real inner product space with Lebesgue measure, and the parameter space AAA is a complete real inner product space. For probability densities q1,…,qMq^1,\dots,q^Mq1,…,qM on EEE, potentials Um:A×E→RU_m:A\times E\to\mathbb RUm​:A×E→R and a parameter aaa, define the normalized density energy, the averaged parameter force and the Fisher information

E(a,q)=1M∑m=1M∫Eqm(log⁡qm+Um(a,⋅)) dz,G(a,q)=1M∑m=1M∫Eqm ∇aUm(a,⋅) dz,\mathcal E(a,q)=\frac1M\sum_{m=1}^M\int_Eq^m(\log q^m+U_m(a,\cdot))\,dz,\qquad G(a,q)=\frac1M\sum_{m=1}^M\int_Eq^m\,\nabla_aU_m(a,\cdot)\,dz,E(a,q)=M1​m=1∑M​∫E​qm(logqm+Um​(a,⋅))dz,G(a,q)=M1​m=1∑M​∫E​qm∇a​Um​(a,⋅)dz, I(a,q)=∥G(a,q)∥2+1M∑m=1M∫Eqm ∥∇z(log⁡qm+Um(a,⋅))∥2 dz.I(a,q)=\|G(a,q)\|^2+\frac1M\sum_{m=1}^M\int_Eq^m\,\bigl\|\nabla_z\bigl(\log q^m+U_m(a,\cdot)\bigr)\bigr\|^2\,dz.I(a,q)=∥G(a,q)∥2+M1​m=1∑M​∫E​qm​∇z​(logqm+Um​(a,⋅))​2dz.

When qmq^mqm is the density of a probability measure QmQ^mQm and the integrals are finite, ∫qm(log⁡qm+Um(a,⋅)) dz=KL(Qm∥πam)−log⁡Zm(a)\int q^m(\log q^m+U_m(a,\cdot))\,dz=\mathrm{KL}(Q^m\|\pi_a^m)-\log Z_m(a)∫qm(logqm+Um​(a,⋅))dz=KL(Qm∥πam​)−logZm​(a), so E(a,q)\mathcal E(a,q)E(a,q) is the free energy F(a,Q)F(a,Q)F(a,Q) of the variational section, written as the paper's literal integral. The flow is the parameter equation a˙t=−G(at,qt)\dot a_t=-G(a_t,q_t)a˙t​=−G(at​,qt​) together with the Fokker–Planck equations ∂tqtm=∇⋅(qtm∇(log⁡qtm+Um(at,⋅)))\partial_tq_t^m=\nabla\cdot\bigl(q_t^m\nabla(\log q_t^m+U_m(a_t,\cdot))\bigr)∂t​qtm​=∇⋅(qtm​∇(logqtm​+Um​(at​,⋅))). The main result is

ddt E(at,qt)=−I(at,qt).\frac{d}{dt}\,\mathcal E(a_t,q_t)=-I(a_t,q_t).dtd​E(at​,qt​)=−I(at​,qt​).

Its proof has three ingredients: differentiation under the integral sign, justified by local domination; Lebesgue integration by parts on the unbounded space EEE, justified by integrability of three explicit products; and the chain rule in the parameter. Along the way we obtain the gradient of E\mathcal EE for the normalized product metric d2=∥a−b∥2+M−1∑mW2(qm,rm)2d^2=\|a-b\|^2+M^{-1}\sum_mW_2(q^m,r^m)^2d2=∥a−b∥2+M−1∑m​W2​(qm,rm)2: its parameter component is GGG and its mmm-th density component is ∇(log⁡qm+Um)\nabla(\log q^m+U_m)∇(logqm+Um​), with no factor 1/M1/M1/M. The identity is used in the convergence theorem for the classical flow; the integration-by-parts identities are also used for the entropy tangent inequality of the transport section.

05Strong displacement convexity of the free energy §

This section proves the strong geodesic convexity of the tilted free energy along displacement interpolations, the paper's Lemma on geodesic convexity, under explicit transport regularity (R4). Let ZZZ be a finite-dimensional real inner product space of dimension ddd, let μ\muμ be a probability measure on ZZZ (the initial law) and let T:Z→ZT:Z\to ZT:Z→Z be a transport map. The displacement interpolation is Ts(z)=(1−s)z+sT(z)T_s(z)=(1-s)z+sT(z)Ts​(z)=(1−s)z+sT(z), s∈[0,1]s\in[0,1]s∈[0,1], and its law is the pushforward μs=μ∘Ts−1\mu_s=\mu\circ T_s^{-1}μs​=μ∘Ts−1​. For one datum, a parameter interpolation ps=(1−s)p0+sp1p_s=(1-s)p_0+sp_1ps​=(1−s)p0​+sp1​ and a joint potential U(p,z)U(p,z)U(p,z), the free energy along the interpolation is

F(s)=H(s)+∫ZU(ps,z) μs(dz),H(s)=∫Zlog⁡ρs dμs,\mathcal F(s)=H(s)+\int_ZU(p_s,z)\,\mu_s(dz),\qquad H(s)=\int_Z\log\rho_s\,d\mu_s,F(s)=H(s)+∫Z​U(ps​,z)μs​(dz),H(s)=∫Z​logρs​dμs​,

where ρs\rho_sρs​ is the Lebesgue density of μs\mu_sμs​ and HHH is the negative Boltzmann entropy. The regularity data consist of positive densities, positive eigenvalues of the Jacobian DTDTDT in an orthonormal eigenbasis, the change-of-variables formula ρs(Ts(z))=ρ0(z)/det⁡((1−s)I+sDT(z))\rho_s(T_s(z))=\rho_0(z)/\det\bigl((1-s)I+sDT(z)\bigr)ρs​(Ts​(z))=ρ0​(z)/det((1−s)I+sDT(z)), and integrable logarithms; no convexity or transport inequality is among them. If UUU is jointly λ\lambdaλ-strongly convex, we prove

F(s)≤(1−s)F(0)+sF(1)−λ2s(1−s)(∥p0−p1∥2+W2(μ0,μ1)2),\mathcal F(s)\le(1-s)\mathcal F(0)+s\mathcal F(1)-\frac\lambda2s(1-s)\bigl(\|p_0-p_1\|^2+W_2(\mu_0,\mu_1)^2\bigr),F(s)≤(1−s)F(0)+sF(1)−2λ​s(1−s)(∥p0​−p1​∥2+W2​(μ0​,μ1​)2),

where W2W_2W2​ is the Wasserstein distance. The entropy part follows from concavity of log⁡det⁡\log\detlogdet; the potential part from joint strong convexity. Consequences are a Talagrand-type quadratic growth at a minimizer and the tangent inequality used for the extended log-Sobolev inequality in the next section.

By (2), c(∥p0−p1∥2+W2(μ,μ1)2)≤c(∥p0−p1∥2+∥id−T∥L2(μ)2)c\bigl(\|p_0-p_1\|^2+W_2(\mu,\mu_1)^2\bigr)\le c\bigl(\|p_0-p_1\|^2+\|\mathrm{id}-T\|_{L^2(\mu)}^2\bigr)c(∥p0​−p1​∥2+W2​(μ,μ1​)2)≤c(∥p0​−p1​∥2+∥id−T∥L2(μ)2​), so the right side of (1) is at most the right side of (3), and (3) follows from (1). □\square□

The map TTT need not be optimal: the conclusion uses the genuine infimum over couplings, which can only be smaller than the cost of TTT. With the normalized product distance of the paper, (3) is the strong geodesic convexity of the free energy of one datum.

06Extended log-Sobolev and Talagrand inequalities §

This section proves the two functional inequalities that drive the convergence of the classical flow: the extended log-Sobolev inequality (the paper's Theorem stating that strong log-concavity implies extended LSI) and a Talagrand-type quadratic growth inequality, both for the normalized free energy of MMM data. The setting is that of the previous section, now for each datum mmm: a probability law QmQ_mQm​ on ZZZ with positive continuously differentiable density ρm\rho_{m}ρm​, regular displacement data TmT_mTm​ from QmQ_mQm​, and a jointly λ\lambdaλ-strongly convex potential UmU_mUm​ on P×ZP\times ZP×Z. With p0p_0p0​ the current parameter, p1p_1p1​ the target parameter and Fm\mathcal F_mFm​ the free energy of datum mmm along the displacement, put F=M−1∑mFm\mathcal F=M^{-1}\sum_m\mathcal F_mF=M−1∑m​Fm​, and define

G=1M∑m∫∇pUm(p0,z) Qm(dz),Sm=∇z(log⁡ρm+Um(p0,⋅)),I=∥G∥2+1M∑m∫∥Sm∥2 dQm.\begin{aligned}G&=\frac1M\sum_m\int\nabla_pU_m(p_0,z)\,Q_m(dz),\\ S_m&=\nabla_z\bigl(\log\rho_m+U_m(p_0,\cdot)\bigr),\\I&=\|G\|^2+\frac1M\sum_m\int\|S_m\|^2\,dQ_m.\end{aligned}GSm​I​=M1​m∑​∫∇p​Um​(p0​,z)Qm​(dz),=∇z​(logρm​+Um​(p0​,⋅)),=∥G∥2+M1​m∑​∫∥Sm​∥2dQm​.​

The main result is 2λ(F(0)−F(1))≤I2\lambda\bigl(\mathcal F(0)-\mathcal F(1)\bigr)\le I2λ(F(0)−F(1))≤I. In the convergence theorem F(0)\mathcal F(0)F(0) is the free energy of the current state and F(1)\mathcal F(1)F(1) that of the posterior optimizer, so this is 2λ(F−F⋆)≤I2\lambda(F-F_\star)\le I2λ(F−F⋆​)≤I. The proof sums two tangent inequalities, one for the entropy (from the Jacobian formula, log⁡x≤x−1\log x\le x-1logx≤x−1 and integration by parts) and one for the potential (from strong convexity), and then completes a square in which the parameter forces are averaged over the data before the norm is squared. No first-order transport inequality or log-Sobolev inequality is assumed.

07Exponential convergence of the continuous flow §

This section proves the paper's continuous-time convergence theorem (Theorem 1 and its appendix form) for classical solutions of the joint gradient flow. The flow consists of a parameter path ata_tat​ and positive densities qt1,…,qtMq_t^1,\dots,q_t^Mqt1​,…,qtM​ solving

a˙t=−1M∑m=1M∫∇aUm(at,z) qtm(z) dz,∂tqtm=∇⋅(qtm∇(log⁡qtm+Um(at,⋅))),\dot a_t=-\frac1M\sum_{m=1}^M\int\nabla_aU_m(a_t,z)\,q_t^m(z)\,dz,\qquad\partial_tq_t^m=\nabla\cdot\bigl(q_t^m\nabla(\log q_t^m+U_m(a_t,\cdot))\bigr),a˙t​=−M1​m=1∑M​∫∇a​Um​(at​,z)qtm​(z)dz,∂t​qtm​=∇⋅(qtm​∇(logqtm​+Um​(at​,⋅))),

together with the regularity of R1–R4: local domination, integrable spatial tails, and, at each time, regular displacement data from the current laws to the laws of a fixed comparison state a⋆a_\stara⋆​. Existence of such a classical solution is not constructed; the estimates hold for every solution in this class. Write E(t)=E(at,qt)−E(a⋆,q⋆)E(t)=\mathcal E(a_t,q_t)-\mathcal E(a_\star,q_\star)E(t)=E(at​,qt​)−E(a⋆​,q⋆​) for the energy gap to the comparison state and dtd_tdt​ for the normalized product distance

dt2=∥at−a⋆∥2+1M∑m=1MW2(qtm,πa⋆m)2.d_t^2=\|a_t-a_\star\|^2+\frac1M\sum_{m=1}^MW_2(q_t^m,\pi_{a_\star}^m)^2.dt2​=∥at​−a⋆​∥2+M1​m=1∑M​W2​(qtm​,πa⋆​m​)2.

When a⋆a_\stara⋆​ maximizes the evidence and the comparison densities are the posteriors πa⋆m\pi_{a_\star}^mπa⋆​m​, we prove

dt≤2E(t)λ≤2E(0)λ e−λt,∥at−a⋆∥≤2E(0)λ e−λt(t≥0).d_t\le\sqrt{\frac{2E(t)}\lambda}\le\sqrt{\frac{2E(0)}\lambda}\,e^{-\lambda t},\qquad\|a_t-a_\star\|\le\sqrt{\frac{2E(0)}\lambda}\,e^{-\lambda t}\qquad(t\ge0).dt​≤λ2E(t)​​≤λ2E(0)​​e−λt,∥at​−a⋆​∥≤λ2E(0)​​e−λt(t≥0).

The ingredients are the de Bruijn identity E′=−IE'=-IE′=−I, the extended log-Sobolev inequality 2λE≤I2\lambda E\le I2λE≤I, Grönwall's inequality, and the Talagrand inequality λ2dt2≤E(t)\frac\lambda2d_t^2\le E(t)2λ​dt2​≤E(t), whose hypothesis (minimality of the posterior state) follows from the Gibbs variational principle. The final theorem constructs a⋆a_\stara⋆​ as the unique maximizer of the evidence of the original potentials, so the only remaining hypotheses are the regularity of the flow.

Let M≥1M\ge1M≥1, λ>0\lambda>0λ>0, and let U1,…,UM:Rdθ×Rdz→RU_1,\dots,U_M:\mathbb R^{d_\theta}\times\mathbb R^{d_z}\to\mathbb RU1​,…,UM​:Rdθ​×Rdz​→R be differentiable and λ\lambdaλ-strongly convex (A3). The theorem contains no assumed dissipation identity, log-Sobolev inequality or transport inequality; the only hypotheses beyond A3 are the regularity conditions defining a classical flow.

08The normalized particle-cloud force §

Let K>0K>0K>0 and let UiU_iUi​ be differentiable potentials on a parameter-latent pair, each mmm-strongly convex with LLL-Lipschitz gradient. Use scaled cloud coordinates z=(a,x1/K,…,xK/K)z=(a,x_1/\sqrt K,\ldots,x_K/\sqrt K)z=(a,x1​/K​,…,xK​/K​). Write Jiz=(a,xi)J_i z=(a,x_i)Ji​z=(a,xi​), V(z)=∑i=1KUi(Jiz)V(z)=\sum_{i=1}^KU_i(J_i z)V(z)=∑i=1K​Ui​(Ji​z), and F(z)=K−1∇V(z)F(z)=K^{-1}\nabla V(z)F(z)=K−1∇V(z). This normalization prevents an artificial deterioration of the monotonicity and smoothness constants when the particle count grows.

Claim. The normalized force FFF is mmm-strongly monotone and LLL-Lipschitz.

Proof. The coordinate maps satisfy ∑i∥Jid∥2=K∥d∥2\sum_i\|J_i d\|^2=K\|d\|^2∑i​∥Ji​d∥2=K∥d∥2: the common parameter square appears KKK times and each scaled latent square is multiplied by KKK. Summing the strong-convexity inequalities for the potentials therefore makes VVV KmKmKm-strongly convex. Differentiability follows by the chain rule and finite summation. For the gradient, the chain rule gives

⟨∇V(x)−∇V(y),w⟩=∑i⟨∇Ui(Jix)−∇Ui(Jiy),Jiw⟩.\langle\nabla V(x)-\nabla V(y),w\rangle=\sum_i\langle\nabla U_i(J_ix)-\nabla U_i(J_iy),J_iw\rangle.⟨∇V(x)−∇V(y),w⟩=i∑​⟨∇Ui​(Ji​x)−∇Ui​(Ji​y),Ji​w⟩.

Lipschitz continuity, Cauchy–Schwarz for the finite sum, and the coordinate identity bound the absolute value by KL∥x−y∥∥w∥KL\|x-y\|\|w\|KL∥x−y∥∥w∥. Taking the supremum over unit vectors gives ∥∇V(x)−∇V(y)∥≤KL∥x−y∥\|\nabla V(x)-\nabla V(y)\|\le KL\|x-y\|∥∇V(x)−∇V(y)∥≤KL∥x−y∥. Strong convexity similarly gives ⟨∇V(x)−∇V(y),x−y⟩≥Km∥x−y∥2\langle\nabla V(x)-\nabla V(y),x-y\rangle\ge Km\|x-y\|^2⟨∇V(x)−∇V(y),x−y⟩≥Km∥x−y∥2. Multiplication by 1/K>01/K>01/K>0 proves both assertions for FFF. The argument allows distinct potentials and arbitrary finite parameter and latent dimensions. □\square□

The division is legitimate because m,h>0m,h>0m,h>0. This proves the bound uniformly in the iteration count. It does not construct the reference path or establish its moment bounds for a new application. □\square□
